title: Are Buffalo Bills worried about Max Hairston, and should they be?
summary: There’s a growing collection of Buffalo Bills fans cornered about Max Hairston. He was the club’s first-round pick in 2025, got injured early in training camp as a rookie but played admirably over the back half of the regular season then injured his ankle in the final game before the playoffs and wasn’t available for […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - AUGUST 22: Maxwell Hairston #31 of the Buffalo Bills walks off the field prior to a preseason game against the Cleveland Browns at Huntington Bank Field on August 22, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images There’s a growing collection of Buffalo Bills fans cornered about Max Hairston. He was the club’s first-round pick in 2025, got injured early in training camp as a rookie but played admirably over the back half of the regular season then injured his ankle in the final game before the playoffs and wasn’t available for either postseason game. To the surprise of most of us, the Bills traded up to use their second selection in the 2026 NFL Draft on an outside cornerback — Davison Igbinosun. In his post-draft presser, Buffalo’s GM Brandon Beane said the following on his cornerbacks: “I got antsy to go get IGB. Well, I was going to try to be patient, but I saw corners going. And I honestly, as we started this draft, thought that was the biggest hole in our roster, was corner.” He later hinted that IGB brings something new to the Bills secondary and spoke to the cornerback pecking order in his mind: “ He’s big, he’s long, and if you look at our two penciled-in starters with Christian Benford and Max [Hairston] right now, those are two different skill sets. I think this is a third skill set. Big, long, the best thing he does is press. Some guys are man match, some guys are best in off, I think he gives us another added skill set.” Those quotes together raised some eyebrows, mostly from skeptics of Hairston. Shouldn’t the former first-round pick have the CB2 job locked down? Frankly, it surprised me a bit too, then I remembered he only appeared on 35.4% of Buffalo’s defensive snaps as a rookie. And now, to some, Hairston has had a bad summer. The three days I was at training camp, I didn’t notice Hairston getting torched. In fact, I saw him make a variety of plays. And he appeared to make positive plays during the Bills-Browns joint practice: Max Hairston denying Denzel Boston, the 6’4”, 215 lb rookie receiver who has been a headline of Browns’ Camp. #BillsMafia pic.twitter.com/cZMXaX4ZsE — Buffalo Sports Talk (@BUFSportsTalk) August 20, 2026 But the point of this article isn’t the argue whether or not Hairston’s had a strong summer or disappointing summer. There’s plenty of subjectivity when evaluating training camp performance. It’s to unpack whether or not the Bills should be concerned about Hairston and his fit in Jim Leonhard’s more man-reliant scheme, especially in the aftermath of this practice-observation tweet from Matt Parrino on Monday that sent many over the edge. If you don’t believe me, check the replies to said tweet: Josh Palmer beat Max Hairston on a deep play that looked like it might go for a TD in 11-on-11 at Bills practice. Hairston pushed Palmer from behind (blatant DPI) & Palmer came up in pain, holding his wrist. Got looked at by trainers and is back in. Josh Allen goes right back… — Matt Parrino (@MattParrino) August 24, 2026 There’s a narrative that Hairston was mostly a zone cornerback at Kentucky. And that’s true. In 2023 with the Wildcats, Hairston played man only 10.9% of his coverage snaps. In 2024, that figure increased but only to 16.9%. Ironically, in 2025, Hairston played man on 26.5% of his coverage snaps, which is a decently high rate in the NFL. Yes, in Sean McDermott’s zone-predicated defense. On those 52 coverage snaps, Hairston allowed just three receptions on six targets in his vicinity with three pass breakups. He didn’t allow a touchdown in man. The internet could argue in perpetuity about “scheme fits” for cornerbacks. I won’t even pretend to know all the technical complexities of playing quality man coverage, particularly in the NFL,. However, from a scouting perspective, twitch, explosiveness, and pure speed are typically the attributes man-coverage specialists have in spades. Those exact attributes jumped off Hairston’s film at Kentucky. What appeared blatantly obvious on his film was quantitatively validated at the 2025 combine. Hairston measured in at 5’11” and 183 pounds and ran 4.28 in the 40-yard dash with a 39.5” vertical and a 10’9” broad jump. He exemplifies the skillset of the modern-day smaller, short-area quicks, and speed-based cornerback. Leonhard did say this to open the week ahead of the final preseason game: #Bills DC Jim Leonhard said the secondary as a whole is a bit concerning because of the lack of reps among the starting group due to injuries. #BillsMafia — Andy Young (@AndyYoungTV) August 24, 2026 Of course, that comment could be partially referring to Hairston, who missed six training camp practices and the first preseason game this summer with a groin injury. Safeties CJ Gardner-Johnson and Cole Bishop were also sidelined for long stretches during camp. Leonhard being “a bit concerned” with the secondary because of lack of reps among the starting group due to injuries wasn’t solely directed at Hairston. Am I worried about Hairston? No. I view him as an ideal high-upside outside cornerback — who can comfortably reduce into the slot — with the suddenness, explosion, and long speed to successfully combat the lightning-quick separators and downfield specialists in today’s NFL. Will there be hiccups along the way in his developmental process? Absolutely. Hairston’s played 348 snaps in the NFL to date and turned 23 earlier this month — he’s hardly a finished product as a professional. I do expect him to emerge as one of the bigger splash-play creators on the Bills defense during the 2026 season. Where do you come down on Hairston before his second season in Buffalo?
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: defensive lineman Deone Walker
summary: With the Buffalo Bills introducing a new defensive scheme this season, there have come questions about how the players on the roster fit new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard’s vision. After former head coach and defensive designer Sean McDermott was fired, the team has seemed to embrace a more physical, aggressive approach in their defensive preparations. […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - AUGUST 15: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers gets sacked by Deone Walker #96 of the Buffalo Bills during the first half at Highmark Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images With the Buffalo Bills introducing a new defensive scheme this season, there have come questions about how the players on the roster fit new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard’s vision. After former head coach and defensive designer Sean McDermott was fired, the team has seemed to embrace a more physical, aggressive approach in their defensive preparations. Rather than relying on sound adherence to place and assignment, the Bills are prioritizing playing quickly as the assignment. One of the positions on the roster that has garnered plenty of discussion is that of the nose tackle. In a 3-down front like Leonhard has implemented, that position is essential to the rest of the defensive line’s success. Truthfully, this isn’t too different from how McDermott’s scheme operated, as the “one-tech” position was analogous to the nost tackle in that it was the spot that allowed the other players on defense to shine. Without a strong player in the middle, the defense is set to struggle. Do the Bills already have that strong player at the nose? In today’s edition of “91 players in 91 days,” we’ll discuss the team’s presumed nose tackle. Spoiler alert: He’s a stud. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Deone Walker Number: 96 Position: DL Height/Weight: 6’7” 331 lbs. Age: 22 (23 on 3/11/2027) Experience/Draft: 2; selected by Buffalo in the fourth round (No. 109 overall) of the 2025 NFL Draft College: Kentucky Acquired: Fourth-round draft choice Financial situation (per Spotrac): Walker enters the second year of his four-year rookie contract, which is worth $5,247,040 overall. In 2026, Walker carries a cap hit of $1,266,760 if he makes the 53-man roster. If he’s released, the Bills will carry a dead cap charge of $785,280. 2025 Recap: After a collegiate season where a back injury limited Walker’s explosiveness, he slid all the way to the fourth round in the 2025 NFL Draft. The Bills scooped him up, and they have reaped the benefits since. Walker was excellent as a rookie, playing in all 17 games and serving as a point of consistency in the middle of a defense wrecked by injuries. Walker totaled 39 tackles, eight tackles for loss, four pass knockdowns, four quarterback hits, one fumble recovery, and one sack during the regular season. He played 464 defensive snaps, good for 47% of the team’s total on defense, as veteran Ed Oliver missed nearly the whole season thanks to a litany of injuries. That snap total was the highest among Bills’ defensive tackles, as veteran DaQuan Jones also missed five games. In the playoffs, Walker was still a wrecking ball, and he put together two very good games. He had six tackles, two pass knockdowns, and an interception while generally wreaking havoc on both the Jacksonville Jaguars and the Denver Broncos. Positional outlook: Walker is set to start at the nose, with DeWayne Carter, Phidarian Mathis (who is suspended for the first three regular season games due to a violation of the NFL’s substance abuse policy), and Zion Logue also playing snaps at that spot. The other defensive linemen on the roster are Tommy Akingbesote, Ed Oliver, Zane Durant, Landon Jackson, Travis Clayton, and T.J. Sanders. 2026 Offseason: Walker is healthy and he has played well this summer. He was only on the field for ten snaps in Buffalo’s preseason opener against the Carolina Panthers, but he was a menace. Walker had a sack, three tackles, two QB pressures, and one tackle for loss. 2026 Season outlook: Buffalo Bills general manager Brandon Beane has done a good job in the middle rounds of his drafts, and it seems like he’s found another mid-round gem in Walker. The big fella is versatile enough where he really could play any role along Jim Leonhard’s three-man front and he’ll find success. That leads to the question of whether the team wants him to be the nose tackle long-term, or do they think it would serve him—and the team—best to play more as a penetrating attacker. If the Bills were looking at Walker as a traditional nose tackle—think Ted Washington—then Walker will be successful. However, he was at his best last season when he was replacing Oliver as the penetrating three-tech player. An overly simple explanation of the difference in roles comes down to gap responsibilities. A one-tech (or zero-tech, as a nose would be considered) is often expected to control more than one blocker as part of his responsibility. As players go farther away from the middle, many defenses ask those linemen to exploit one-on-one matchups, and those matchups are often exploitable because of the success of the big fella in the middle. Leonhard’s defense seems to be less concerned about the gap assignments and more concerned with causing chaos in opposing backfields. That should give Walker (and the rest of Buffalo’s defensive line) plenty of freedom to make plays. That freedom was on full display during Buffalo’s preseason opener, and while any exhibition results should be digested with caution, there were plenty of reasons to be optimistic. Walker, both literally and figuratively, was one of the biggest reasons for optimism. So long as Walker stays healthy, he’s going to have a huge role on the Bills’ defense this season. If his early play is any indication, he might become a household name sooner rather than later.

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 19 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TN - NOVEMBER 4: Kicker John Kasay #4 of the Carolina Panthers kicks a field goal in a game against the Tennessee Titans at LP Field on November 4, 2007 in Nashville, Tennessee. The Titans defeated the Panthers 20-6. (Photo by Tim Umphrey/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #19. John Kasay In the fourth round of the 1991 NFL Draft, the Seattle Seahawks drafted the player who would eventually become the all time leading scorer for the Carolina Panthers. Unlike previous players on the list who had immensely high peaks with limited career lengths in Carolina, John Kasay is a testament to longevity. After spending four years with Seattle, he signed with the Panthers prior to the 1995 season. Just like the Panthers themselves, Kasay really burst on the scene in 1996, setting career highs in field goals made (37) and field goals attempted (45) and earning a Pro Bowl nod and Second Team All-Pro honors. Kasay hit a rough patch injury-wise in 1999, tearing his ACL trying to make a tackle in a December game against the Green Bay Packers. Kasay worked to return the following season, just eight months after the injury, before fracturing his kneecap in training camp by basically kicking too hard. Literally, the force of his quadriceps contracting basically snapped his kneecap in two on a basic 30 yard field goal attempt at practice. Kasay was having arguably his best season in ‘99, and he came back pretty strong in 2001 following almost a year and a half off the field due to injuries. That string continued in 2002, when a sports hernia in his groin ended his season after just two games. Then came the 2003 season. Back and fully healthy, Kasay was relied on multiple times in the clutch as the Panthers made their first Super Bowl appearance. During the regular season, Kasay nailed four game winning kicks, including three in overtime (Week 2 in Tampa, Week 6 in Indianapolis, and Week 8 in New Orleans) and one as time expired (Week 13 at home against the Falcons). In the playoffs, Kasay kept the Panthers in games they ended up winning and put himself in the postseason record books by tying a playoff record with five made field goals against the Cowboys and the (at the time) third longest field goal in Super Bowl history (50 yards just before halftime). The 2004 season was the last time Kasay missed any games due to injury, straining his right calf and missing two games that year. Still, the injuries played a role in his diminishing leg strength. Once the team realized he wasn’t going to bounce back from 50+, Kasay had some of the best accuracy numbers of his career, including his career best 90.3% during the 2008 season. He also made all of his career-high 46 extra point attempts that year. As for many players and coaches on the Panthers, the 2010 season was Kasay’s last with the organization. He signed a one year deal with the Saints, played well, then signed a one day contract with Carolina to retire as a Panther in 2011. Kasay’s longevity and steadiness is something many fans may have underrated at the time. Think about the Olindo Mare years, and suddenly Kasay is amazing. While he wasn’t without his faults and miscues (cough, Super Bowl kickoff out of bounds, cough), you can’t tell the history of the Panthers without including him. He was a premier contributor in two of the team’s best seasons (1996 and 2003) and is still ninth in NFL history in points scored with 1,970 over the course of his 20 year NFL career. The reliable left leg of John Kasay earned him No. 19 spot in our countdown of greatest Panthers ever.

title: Report: Bears fielding trade calls on DT Gervon Dexter

Schultz previously reported in February that teams were calling on Dexter’s availability around the time of the 2026 NFL Scouting […]
full_text: The Chicago Bears have been involved in trade discussions surrounding defensive tackle, NFL insider Jordan Schultz reported on Tuesday. Dexter, who turns 25 in October, is currently in the final year of his rookie contract. Schultz previously reported in February that teams were calling on Dexter’s availability around the time of the 2026 NFL Scouting Combine. Now, Schultz is claiming that there are “multiple scenarios where a deal could get done”. Dexter was a second-round pick in the 2023 NFL Draft coming out of Florida. He is coming off a 2025 campaign in which he tallied 44 tackles, 6.0 tackles for loss, and a career-high 6.0 sacks. He placed No. 32 among 107 qualified defensive tackles in PFN DT Impact Scoring , a ranking which indicates he’s an average starting defensive tackle. That said, his pass-rushing production and youth gives him considerable upside on the open market. Should the Bears actually trade Dexter, they would free up over $1.6 million in 2026 cap space . The reason to trade Dexter wouldn’t be highlighted by the immediate cap relief, but rather, the draft capital Chicago could obtain in a deal. If the team realizes they likely won’t extend him at the price he and his agency are asking for, it could make sense in the long run to get a draft pick for him, rather than let him walk in free agency for nothing. Of course, the Bears’ defensive line has been the subject of much discussion leading up to the 2026-27 NFL season. Their four-man front consistently struggled to generate pressure in the pass rush and had issues in run support, and they didn’t do much to address the need this offseason. Trading Dexter would certainly weaken their interior defensive line and thrust the likes of Neville Gallimore, Kentavius Street, and sixth-round pick Jordan van den Berg into bigger roles alongside Grady Jarrett, who is coming off a disappointing 2025 season.

full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 10: Elijah Hicks #22 of the Chicago Bears reacts following an NFL wild card playoff game against the Green Bay Packers at Soldier Field on January 10, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Earlier today, the Chicago Bears activated rookie linebacker Keyshaun Elliott and safety Elijah Hicks off the Active/Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list. The Bears still have three players on the PUP list: Nickelback Kyler Gordon, linebacker Noah Sewell, and defensive lineman Shemar Turner. They also placed linebacker Nephi Sewell on injured reserve and signed linebacker Antonio Grier. Nephi Sewell was carted off during Saturday’s preseason game in Cincinnati. The 26-year-old Grier (6’1”, 230) was originally a 2024 UDFA from Arkansas who signed by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. He played 7 games with them as a rookie, mostly on special teams. He was waived/injured before the 2025 season, and he spent time with the Louisville Kings of the United Football League in 2026. The Bears close out the preseason on Saturday against the Tennessee Titans, and this year’s cut-down deadline is Sunday at 5:00 pm (CT).

title: Five Bears Takes Following Their Preseason Week 2 Game In Cincinnati
summary: On Saturday evening, the Chicago Bears hosted the Cincinnati Bengals in one of those preseason contests that everyone struggles to get through. Despite the starters getting time in the first quarter, there wasn’t much to write home about, which can be both good and bad. With one more game remaining in the preseason and roster […]
full_text: Aug 22, 2026; Cincinnati, Ohio, USA; Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams (18) snaps the ball against the Cincinnati Bengals in the first half at Paycor Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Katie Stratman-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect On Saturday evening, the Chicago Bears hosted the Cincinnati Bengals in one of those preseason contests that everyone struggles to get through. Despite the starters getting time in the first quarter, there wasn’t much to write home about, which can be both good and bad. With one more game remaining in the preseason and roster cuts to follow shortly after, the next seven days are going to be hectic for every team around the league. Before we officially turn the page on a tough-to-watch game in Cincinnati, let’s dive into five thoughts following the Bears’ 27-9 preseason loss. 1. Despite a practice last Sunday designed for starters and the joint practice in Cincy, the Bears opted to give their starters a brief look on Saturday night. While it may not be easy to remember, head coach Ben Johnson and the coaching staff followed a similar script in last year’s preseason slate. They had an eventful day of joint practices, followed by the starting offense playing roughly 15 snaps. Although things didn’t go the same this season, quarterback Caleb Williams and the offense were on the field for eight plays, picking up 33 yards, and despite a 1st and 10 from the Bengals’ 17, they settled for a field goal before giving their starters the rest of the night (and likely preseason) off. All in all, there wasn’t much to write home about on either side of the ball. The defense is more banged up, which led to fewer projected Week 1 starters, but once the starters were set, it was a 3-3 game. The offense showed flashes, including Williams completing his first two passes for 28 yards, before finishing the drive with three straight incompletions, one of which was batted down. For the first time in what feels like forever, there wasn’t much for the Bears to prove during the preseason. As we’ve learned over the years, it’s rare for much to translate over from the preseason to the regular season anyway. It’s easy to live in the moment, and for that, we’ve seen plenty of takes surrounding Williams’ miss to Colston Loveland near the end zone. That being said, this was more about the process of getting ready for a game, and much less about the meaningless results of a game that doesn’t count in the record books. While I’ve got no problem with each unit’s starters getting a series, I hope that Saturday night will be about the bottom end of the roster. 2. With Braxton Jones back healthy and a switch-up at practice last week, it appears that the left tackle battle is settled for now. Whether that’s a good or a bad thing is yet to be determined, but barring Ozzy Trapilo being physically ready to play Week 1, the only viable starting option seems to be Jones. Coming off the heels of a rough preseason performance last Saturday, it’s fair for fans to be a little skeptical. Admittedly, I am too. Jones’ lack of an anchor continues to be an issue in his pass sets, and despite him being healthy, he doesn’t appear to have the same lateral movement that he did before last season. The bigger issue is that the competition behind him has been about as bad as it gets. Barring a surprise, Kiran Amegadjie’s three-year tenure in Chicago is most likely coming to an end. Despite the upside gamble, it seems clear that Jedrick Wills Jr. is simply not back to 100% physically, and I’m not sure the Bears can afford to wait around on him to get there. Because of that, the coaching staff swapped both players to the right side, while giving Theo Benedet one last crack at the left tackle job. The key is that the team made it pretty clear they had little interest in seeing Benedet on the left side again, which should tell you everything you need to know about how they feel about Amegadjie and Wills. The general expectation is still that Trapilo will end up on Injured Reserve for the first four-to-six games of the season. While they might disappoint some, getting him back for any time this season should be viewed as a plus. The goal needs to be getting him into physical and mental shape to play football and do it at a higher level than Jones (or whoever has the job by then). Assuming Trapilo isn’t on the active roster, it’s looking more and more like the Bears might keep just nine offensive linemen, including just three tackles on the final roster. 3. Three roster bubble names I feel good about making the team. iOL Jordan McFadden WR Kaden Davis LB Jack Sanborn Heading into camp, I wasn’t sure how many offensive linemen the Bears would keep and how many of them would be tackles. Given how that competition has played out, it seems entirely possible the team could keep nine players on the depth chart and only one at tackle (Benedet). If so, that leaves Logan Jones, Luke Newman, and likely McFadden as the final three to claim spots. With Thuney not playing last Saturday, it was once again McFadden receiving the nod at left guard. That speaks volumes about where the team sees him, especially after their decision in the divisional round back in January. Davis is a player I had firmly on the outside looking in as camp opened up. Still, considering his special teams value and his playmaking ability in almost every practice session, it feels like a worthwhile argument that he’s done more to earn a final roster spot than anyone else on the depth chart around him. Although I wouldn’t consider him a lock, I’d consider him the favorite heading into the final week of preseason action. Finally, we have Sanborn, who is in his second stint with the Bears. Originally, he was projected as a fringe player because of his lack of speed. That said, injuries and a lack of standout play around him have Sanborn firmly in the driver’s seat for one of the final spots on the depth chart come next Sunday. Athletically, he profiles similarly to TJ Edwards at this point in his career, and while I have concerns about him starting more than a game or two, Sanborn also brings quality special teams value. 4. Three roster bubble names that I don’t think will be on the roster come Sunday night. CB Terell Smith DT Kentavius Street WR Scotty Miller Every year before the start of training camp, everyone puts out projected 53-man rosters, and in the moment, it feels so “easy,” right? Projecting injuries is impossible, which makes this exercise like throwing darts at a dartboard. Still, even then, you assume most players will survive the preseason and, in the end, the obvious parts of the roster will pan out the way you expected. For the Bears, there might not be many surprises, but with five players still on the PUP list and others like Coby Bryant slated to miss a large chunk of the regular season, it gets a little more interesting. That being said, players like Smith, who haven’t proven their ability to stay on the field when it matters, might just find themselves on the outside looking in on Sunday. Cornerback is a tough spot, especially with the status of Gordon and Tyrique Stevenson (week-to-week) still up in the air heading into Week 1. That’s why keeping players like Smith, who have struggled to stay on the field since they were drafted, might not make a lot of sense. Moving down the list, Street was signed early in the offseason and projected as a bubble player, even if I would have classified him “leaning in” when camp opened. That said, there hasn’t been much to write home about, and with the emergence of sixth-round rookie Jordan van den Berg and even veteran James Lynch, Street feels like a player that might be easier to slide on the practice squad for some additional depth. Finally, there’s Miller. I would have probably deemed him the “favorite” for the WR6 job, although I wasn’t convinced they would end up keeping six on the final roster. As training camp and the preseason have played out,…

full_text: Saturday night was a fun one in the Queen City as the Cincinnati Bengals defeated the Chicago Bears 27-9 during preseason game two. While the Bengals’ second-round draft selection, Cashius Howell, did not play, we still saw fantastic performances from other draft picks from this past April. Tacario Davis The Bengals selected Davis with the 72nd overall selection in the third round. The physical attributes immediately stand out for a cornerback. Davis is 6’4”, 194 pounds, and ran in the 4.4’s in the 40-yard dash. While some of the change-of-direction ability in coverage can leave a bit to be desired, this is a physical presence playing at outside corner. Davis didn’t waste any time getting physical against the run on Saturday night. Davis finished the game with 7 tackles, including some big plays near or behind the line of scrimmage. For a team that has struggled with missed tackles, it was refreshing to see a player who consistently wrapped up and embraced the physical part of playing defense. Tacario Davis showed off his physicality in his Bengals debut against the Bears pic.twitter.com/DJkjK6OTjO — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) August 23, 2026 Landon Robinson Robinson continued making splash plays in the second preseason game against the Bears. He finished the game with 3 tackles, 1.5 sacks, and a pass defensed at the line. This guy is built like a fire hydrant. He has the strength to maintain gap integrity, but his bread and butter is what he does rushing the passer. His closing burst, relentless effort in pursuit, and natural leverage all allow him to be a consistent headache for opposing offenses. I can’t see how the Bengals keep him off the 53-man roster. Not only would I have him on the roster, but I would also have him active on gamedays. He can play fullback on the goal line, could add value on special teams, and even if just as a rotational pass rusher, I think he would make an impact this year if given the opportunity. Robinson has done everything right, and we all know that the Naval Academy graduate will not be outworked. Landon Robinson with another standout performance on Saturday night. pic.twitter.com/4bOMXTp9RU — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) August 23, 2026 Jack Dingle Dingle wasn’t a draft selection, but was quickly signed as an undrafted free agent. After not hearing much about him throughout camp, it was nice to see him making plays. The former Cincinnati Bearcat is trying to solidify a spot on the practice squad this season. If he can be able to do that and stick around, he could potentially be a player down the road that they develop into a rotational player and special teams guy. title: Bengals Tuesday Trenches: The 3 biggest needs heading into Preseason Week 3
summary: Week 2 of the preseason is in the books. If the Cincinnati Bengals’ Week 1 16-14 win over the Lions got you excited, then their 27-9 win over the Bears this past Saturday really got your blood pumping. It’s easy to look too far into preseason games, on both positive and negative performances, but here […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals guard Orlando Brown Jr. laughs on the sideline in the fourth quarter of the NFL Preseason game between the Cincinnati Bengals and the Detroit Lions at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati on Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. The Bengals won the preseason opener, 16-14. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Week 2 of the preseason is in the books. If the Cincinnati Bengals ’ Week 1 16-14 win over the Lions got you excited, then their 27-9 win over the Bears this past Saturday really got your blood pumping. It’s easy to look too far into preseason games, on both positive and negative performances, but here are some quick takeaways from Saturday : The Bengals did not play their starters, and the Bears did (very briefly). The Bengals’ defense kept the Bears out of the end zone for the entire game. Both Josh Johnson and Sean Clifford moved the ball well. Landon Robinson had a game, and the Bengals’ defensive tackle rotation is going to be deep. Evan McPherson has been money all preseason, and was good from 58 and 25 yards on Saturday. The Bengals not only have the best wide receiver duo in the league (and it’s not close), but they have the best overall wide receiver room in the NFL (and it’s not close). It wasn’t all sunshine and rainbows. The backup offensive line and overall offensive line depth are not good. Cody Ford was so bad on Saturday night (0.0 pass-blocking score on 30 reps) that the Bengals released him on Monday, a week before final cuts need to be made. So there are things that need some work. With one preseason game left before the 53-man roster needs to be finalized, here are three things IN ORDER the Bengals need to do: 1. Find a new swing tackle Ford has played every position other than center for the Bengals, and a big reason he hung around here as long as he did was because of his versatility. He’s been the team’s swing tackle, the backup that can play left or right tackle should a starter go down, but on Saturday night he started at right guard, and he was bad. The Bengals started Javon Foster at left tackle, and Brian Parker II at right tackle, and neither inspired confidence that they could be relied upon should an injury occur. So the Bengals need to find a tackle they can trust. Both Orlando Brown Jr and Amarius Mims are big guys, and they’ve both dealt with injuries in the past. With only 17 games in a season, the Bengals don’t have the luxury of rolling the dice that they won’t need a backup tackle. The options in free agency are limited at this point, but all 32 teams will need to make cuts to get their rosters down to 53—there will be guys available. Should they wait, though? They could make a trade. They are going to cut a defensive lineman who could be in a solid rotation elsewhere. They’re going to cut someone’s future WR3. They could trade someone now if they were really wanting to blow everyone’s mind with two trades in one offseason. Or they could sign Jonah Williams. 2. Cornerback The Bengals didn’t do much at the position this offseason. They did sign Ja’Sir Taylor in free agency to a one-year deal, and they selected Tacario Davis in the third round. They’re heading into the season with Dax Hill, DJ Turner, and Jalen Davis penciled in as the starters, and they have Taylor and DJ Ivey to call upon. They could really use another veteran cornerback in the room. They don’t even need someone to push for starting time, but just someone to be there if the worst were to happen. Hill is working his way back from a training camp injury, and he’s expected to be ready for the beginning of the year, but some injuries can be nagging. Being too prepared is not a bad thing. 3. Linebacker A couple of weeks ago, this would have been at the top of the list, but I’m so encouraged by what I’ve seen from the defensive front that this is now a lower priority. There will be a trickle-down effect from an offensive line so overwhelmed with the four men in front of them that they can’t focus on the two or three trying to diagnose the play. Do you remember how good Logan Wilson and Germaine Pratt were when DJ Reader was soaking up blockers in front of them? There was a reason their play declined when he left. A linebacker’s ability to diagnose a play and get himself in position quickly can be aided by a mountain of a nose tackle keeping the center and guard focused on him. Having said that, Barrett Carter and Demetrius Knight Jr. were the worst starting linebacker duo in the league last year. They’ll have a year of experience under their belt, and they now have a vastly improved defensive line in front of them, but they could benefit from a veteran in the room. They have Joe Giles-Harris and Oren Burks, but their backups could use an upgrade. In my opinion, if the Bengals were definitely going to do just ONE of these things, it has to be signing an offensive tackle. They’ve done such a good job at swinging for the fences this offseason, and they cannot get it undone by an offensive tackle injury that, in turn, could lead to a quarterback injury. The defense is much improved, but Joe Burrow is, has been, and will be the key. If he’s healthy, they have a chance. If the Bengals can’t protect him, they risk everything. What do you think? What are your top three needs, in order, as the Bengals prepare to visit the Eagles in the City of Brotherly Love on Friday night? Sound off! Then we get a week off, and then the real deal begins. summary: As tight end C.J. Uzomah calls it a career, we take some time to remember his time with the Cincinnati Bengals. full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - FEBRUARY 07: C.J. Uzomah #87 of the Cincinnati Bengals speaks during a Cincinnati Bengals Fan Rally ahead of Super Bowl LVI at Paul Brown Stadium on February 07, 2022 in Cincinnati, Ohio. He was one of the biggest leaders in the 2021 season, and as early as the beginning of the year, he was saying, “Why not us?” when competing for a championship. That 2021 season was one no Bengals fans will forget. Truly one of the best times to be a fan of this team. He was taken in the fifth round of the 2015 draft. After his best year with the team in 2021, he went to the New York Jets for two seasons before landing with the Philadelphia Eagles in 2024, where he got a Super Bowl ring playing a depth role. Thanks for the memories, C.J. pic.twitter.com/NonifCmBhV — Cincinnati Bengals (@Bengals) August 24, 2026 Easily one of his most memorable games was the team’s coming-out party against the Baltimore Ravens in 2021. Here are the highlights from that game: #5 largest upset of 2021: week 7: 4-2 Bengals @ 5-1 Ravens Bengals were a 6 point underdog Bengals won 41-17, covering by 30 pts Ja'Marr Chase: 8 rec, 201 yds, TD Joe Burrow: 23-38, 416 yds, 3 TD, INT CJ Uzomah: 3 rec, 91 yds, 2 TD pic.twitter.com/HoE8QCUcV6 — Warren Sharp (@SharpFootball) June 1, 2022 Bengals News Training Camp Report: C.J. Uzomah Returns To His Who-Dey Home To Retire, But He’ll Be Around Now Uzomah is no longer a Bengals’ trivia question. He’s part of the fabric with the news that he’ll begin retirement as a contributor to Bengals media this season. Uzomah is slated to be a guest host with Dan Hoard on Bengals Weekly in a rotating role with Tony Pike and Joe Danneman. He’ll also be working on selected radio shows during the week. The Bengals put it out there, and Uzomah went for it even though he always thought no one wanted to hear his voice. Uzomah will make a very entertaining media person. He certainly has the personality from it, but even during his time with the team, you could tell that he knew the game very well. 2026 Cincinnati Bengals: Projecting final 53-man roster Meyers, the former CFL signee, was impressive throughout training camp and made a strong impression on everyone in the building. That gives him the edge over Charlie Jones, who is one of the best returners in the NFL. 53-man roster predictions are going to be spicy this year. Looking at the wide receiver, defensive tackle and tight end rooms alone are probably three of the tightest contests we’ve seen in years for roster spots. Bengals Could Fix Big Weakness With Recently Released Free Agent The Arizona Cardinals waived Trey Benson with an injury designation on Monday. If Benson clears waivers, he will revert to Arizona’s injured reserve. The Bengals should at least consider placing a claim on the former third-round pick. The running back depth could be better. Benson likely reverting back to the Cardinals with an injury designation certainly seems like a very likely outcome. This team does not like to gamble on players who have had availability issues in the NFL. That being said, he would be a great running mate with Chase Brown down the road. NFL News Christian McCaffrey: Absence from practices was ‘part of the plan from the jump’ With McCaffrey sitting out practices, rumors began to fly. From questions about his injury status to speculation that his absence was contract-related. Interestingly, the 49ers’ brass could have simply said the RB’s absence was a plan of sorts from the beginning, but did not. McCaffrey dismissed the stories and noted that sometimes he needs to be protected from his own competitive nature. McCaffrey hitting the field again is great news. You have to hope this guy can put it together at least one more time for an entire season. He is definitely getting towards the end of his time in the NFL, but he might have one good year left to go out with a bang. NFL Network: Patriots agree to trade WR Kayshon Boutte to Texans The Texans are acquiring wideout Kayshon Boutte in a trade with the New England Patriots, NFL Network Insider Ian Rapoport reported Monday. Houston is sending safety Jaylen Reed and a 2028 seventh-round pick to New England in exchange for Boutte. A player for player trade happening might give some inspiration for Cincinnati to pull the trigger with all these quality players they could be forced to cut. But the Texans may have gotten slightly better, which is noteworthy if the Bengals return to being a competitor. Mike McCarthy: Steelers at contract ‘impasse’ with CB Joey Porter Jr. Porter is in the final season of the four-year deal he signed after the Steelers selected him with the first pick of the second round in 2023. While Pittsburgh has locked up other members of that draft class — including outside linebacker Nick Herbig and tight end Darnell Washington — Porter’s status seems a little more uncertain. What a poverty franchise. Can you imagine your team not paying a top player at their position? Man the Rooney family is really struggling with money, huh? No wonder this team doesn’t have a franchise quarterback. What quarterback would willingly stay as they fight their best players over contracts?

title: Bengals offensive rookie roundup vs. Chicago Bears
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals defeated the Chicago Bears 27-9 on Saturday night at Paycor Stadium. While none of the projected starters played during the game, there were plenty of backups that showed they deserve a spot on the Bengals’ 53-man roster. Connor Lew Lew made his debut on Saturday night. This was his first game action […]
full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals defeated the Chicago Bears 27-9 on Saturday night at Paycor Stadium. While none of the projected starters played during the game, there were plenty of backups that showed they deserve a spot on the Bengals’ 53-man roster. Connor Lew Lew made his debut on Saturday night. This was his first game action since tearing his ACL in October while playing at Auburn. He played in only 18 total snaps on the night, but showed exactly why many people viewed him as a top 50 prospect prior to injury. Lew has good athleticism, is a high-intelligence football player, and will not even turn 21 years old until August 30th. The Bengals have Ted Karras as their starting center for 2026, but Connor Lew is the center of the future. Landing him with a fourth-round draft selection will end up feeling like highway robbery. This guy is going to be a good one. It was good seeing Connor Lew back in live game action for the first time since tearing his ACL on October 20th last year. The Bengals getting him in the 4th round was a steal. pic.twitter.com/nUOgIfBsew — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) August 23, 2026 Colbie Young The Bengals’ second selection in the fourth round was Colbie Young. He was impressive again this week. Finishing the game with three receptions, 48 yards, and a receiving touchdown. This guy has shown that he is a consistent chain mover, just like he was in college. His ability to gear down at the top of his breaks as a route runner with his size is a sight to behold. The Bengals did not play Andrei Iosivas at all during the game, signaling that he will once again start the season as a starter at wide receiver. I have a hard time seeing him keeping that job all season long. Young and Dohnte Meyers should both get opportunities, and when they do, I think we’ll see a lot more Colbie Young as the year progresses. Either way, Young will have opportunities this season, and he looks like a player with a bright future in Cincinnati. It didn’t take long for Colbie Young to make an impact for the Bengals, picking up the first down here to keep the chains moving. Have been really impressed with his route running and how he tempos his routes, along with the really strong hands he is known for. pic.twitter.com/J61UgIUZ3p — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) August 23, 2026 Colbie Young winning off the line for the touchdown pic.twitter.com/PjJQuLYmWO — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) August 23, 2026 Brian Parker II I thought Bengals sixth-round selection Brian Parker II looked the part of a future starting offensive lineman again this week. He took snaps at both left and right guard, a week after playing both left guard and center. Primarily a right tackle at Duke, versatility is the calling card for Parker this upcoming season for the Bengals. As he continues getting used to playing more on the interior, he has the luxury to learn from veterans like Ted Karras and Dalton Risner. That should only help him in the future. Already, he looks like a player who could start in Cincinnati for many, many years to come. Brian Parker II looked the part again on Saturday versus the Bears. Has now taken snaps at all three interior spots during the preseason, and played tackle in college. Valuable depth for this season, and a future starter. pic.twitter.com/cqrhd6Q5Wi — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) August 24, 2026 Jack Endries Endries didn’t have as big of a standout performance catching the ball as he did during the first preseason game. He finished the night with just one reception for 7 yards. He was targeted three times during the night, with one of them turning into an underthrow that was intercepted by the Bears. He did finish the night with some respectable blocking grades, with a 67.6 pass-blocking grade and a 61.1 run-blocking grade. Endries is still in a battle to make the 53-man roster. If the Bengals elect to keep just four tight ends, the final spot will likely come down to either Endries or Tanner Hudson. Hudson finished the night with two receptions for 17 yards and a receiving touchdown. I still feel like Endries finds his way on the roster, but a bigger game in the preseason finale on Thursday would boost his case even more.

summary: For a player who went undrafted in the 2026 NFL Draft and was waived by the Philadelphia Eagles before being claimed by the Cleveland Browns, TE Dae’Quan Wright has become a big name in the story of football. While one of our astute readers was very excited when the Browns claimed Wright, his odds of […]
full_text: Sep 27, 2025; Oxford, Mississippi, USA; Mississippi Rebels tight end Dae'Quan Wright (8) catches the ball during the third quarter against the LSU Tigers at Vaught-Hemingway Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Petre Thomas-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect For a player who went undrafted in the 2026 NFL Draft and was waived by the Philadelphia Eagles before being claimed by the Cleveland Browns, TE Dae’Quan Wright has become a big name in the story of football. While one of our astute readers was very excited when the Browns claimed Wright , his odds of making the team’s initial 53-man roster were low, but the lack of depth at his position might have helped. Instead, Wright was a part of a lawsuit that deemed he could return to college , despite another legal ruling seemingly stopping that, and was waived by Cleveland to make a “history” making move to LSU possible . On Tuesday, Wright cleared waivers and was set to join Lane Kiffin’s Tigers: As the immortal Lee Corso would say, “Not so fast, my friends.“ The SEC joined the Big 10 in passing a policy that would lead to LSU receiving penalties if they had Wright, or any other player who met the three provisions of the policy, on their roster: Following meetings with the Presidents, Chancellors, and Athletics Directors of the Southeastern Conference, the SEC will enforce the following policy: pic.twitter.com/LohWnb7G1J — Southeastern Conference (@SEC) August 25, 2026 As former Green Bay Packers executive Andrew Brandt is fond of saying, “There will be lawyers.” As for Wright returning to the Browns, anything is possible, as he is now an NFL (and potentially college) free agent. Given the timing, even if Wright signs with an NFL team, it is highly unlikely to be on a 53-man roster; instead, the athletic tight end would likely end up on a practice squad. Then again, Wright’s story has already had lots of twists and turns; perhaps he tries to transfer to a school in a conference that hasn’t yet passed a rule like the Big 10 and SEC. Given the wild swings so far, a return to Cleveland is likely an option as well. What do you think of all of this? Is it just a blip on the radar or a bigger issue for football in general? title: NFL trades: 3 roster positions the Browns should be looking to upgrade
summary: While NFL free agency is ongoing until the end of the Super Bowl, the Cleveland Browns and the rest of the NFL are mostly scraping the bottom of the barrel at this point in time in the season. Sure, RB Kareem Hunt might be able to help a team like the Detroit Lions, and the […]
full_text: Cleveland Browns general manager Andrew Berry watches drills during the first day of rookie minicamp May 8, 2026, at Cross Country Mortgage Campus in Berea, Ohio. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co While NFL free agency is ongoing until the end of the Super Bowl, the Cleveland Browns and the rest of the NFL are mostly scraping the bottom of the barrel at this point in time in the season. Sure, RB Kareem Hunt might be able to help a team like the Detroit Lions , and the Browns are hoping that DE Derek Barnett helps offset the loss of DE Alex Wright , but there are reasons that players are still available on the NFL free-agent market. NFL trade rumors could start to swirl as teams prepare for cutdown day, with Cleveland’s Thursday Night contest giving them a bit of a head start . If the free agent market doesn’t have answers, teams may look to swap positions of depth to help fill positions of weakness before starting preparation for Week 1 of the 2026 NFL regular season. A look at a 53-man roster projection for the Browns seems to indicate some obvious holes that could be filled on the trade market. Three positions stand out with depth concerns: Tight end Harold Fannin Jr. is a great young starting point, but after that, Cleveland is looking at a career journeyman (Blake Whiteheart) and a late-round rookie ( Carsen Ryan ) to fill the rest of the depth chart. The NFL is not full of a lot of tight ends ready to play meaningful snaps who are also available in a trade, but GM Andrew Berry will likely make some calls. Defensive end Berry has been looking for edge help since training camp started, with Barnett coming in to offset Wright’s injury. Any and every defensive end that could hit the waiver wire or free agent market might instead end up on the Browns roster via a trade. Cornerback With Denzel Ward and Tyson Campbell , Cleveland’s cornerback room is set at the top. The Browns seem convinced that Myles Harden can handle the slot corner spot but, beyond that, there are a lot of questions. DC Mike Rutenberg could end up playing a lot of three safeties to offset the corner need if Berry can’t bring in any help. Besides quarterback, which has been the big conversation all offseason, where do you have the most concern on the Browns roster and do you expect them to fill it with a trade? Join the conversation! title: Browns DT ready to end his ‘long journey’ and get back to playing
summary: The Cleveland Browns made all kinds of headlines on Monday with the news that veteran Deshaun Watson is head coach Todd Monken’s choice to be the starting quarterback this fall. While the Watson news consumed all the oxygen in Browns Town, he is not the only injured veteran set to make a return to the […]
full_text: DT Maliek Collins #96 (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cleveland Browns made all kinds of headlines on Monday with the news that veteran Deshaun Watson is head coach Todd Monken’s choice to be the starting quarterback this fall. While the Watson news consumed all the oxygen in Browns Town , he is not the only injured veteran set to make a return to the field, as the team also activated defensive tackle Maliek Collins from the physically unable to perform list. Collins has been out since suffering a season-ending quad injury during Cleveland’s Week 15 game against the San Francisco 49ers last November. Finally healthy, Collins was back on the practice field on Monday and met with the media on Tuesday to share his excitement at being back with the team : “It felt good, man. It’s a blessing to be able to get back out there. I guess it’s been a long journey coming back, but it really ain’t been that long, man. It’s just really been an off-season and just recovering, getting my body back right to be able to go play.” Before his injury, Collins was enjoying life playing between Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett and rookie Mason Graham. Collins had posted a career-high 6.5 sacks to go along with 13 quarterback hits and seven tackles for loss. Maliek Collins has high expectations pic.twitter.com/337MiepYwD — Cleveland Browns (@Browns) August 25, 2026 But even though his numbers were good, Collins believes he still could have played better : “It’s probably the most production I’ve had. I don’t think it’s as well as I’ve played, but it’s probably the most productive for sure. I think I’ve had better film. I think I was super productive, but I think I’ve had better film for sure.” Like everyone else on the defense, Collins will have to adjust without Garrett taking up two and three blockers at a time. But he sees good things from defensive end Jared Verse, the man tasked with replacing Garrett on the defensive line: “Playing next to Jared has been great. Interaction, seeing him, how he does team stuff, how he is in our room, I think it’s been great.” The depth at defensive tackle is a bit thin behind Graham, although Mike Hall Jr. staying healthy will certainly help. As will having a veteran like Collins back in the huddle, as everyone will need to step up their play to make up for the absence of Garrett. Even if his return was overshadowed by the quarterback news.

title: Browns 53-man roster projection: The tough calls, weak positions, deep spots
summary: For at least three to four weeks, the Cleveland Browns have made a decision about the quarterback competition. Gone are the QB trackers, the reasons Deshaun Watson or Shedeur Sanders should/shouldn’t get the job, and pondering what the team will look like with each quarterback. That doesn’t mean the media and fans will stop talking […]
full_text: BEREA, OHIO - JUNE 09: Executive vice president, football operations & general manager Andrew Berry of the Cleveland Browns watches a drill during the Cleveland Browns Mandatory Minicamp at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus on June 09, 2026 in Berea, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images For at least three to four weeks, the Cleveland Browns have made a decision about the quarterback competition. Gone are the QB trackers, the reasons Deshaun Watson or Shedeur Sanders should/shouldn’t get the job, and pondering what the team will look like with each quarterback. That doesn’t mean the media and fans will stop talking about it, but the team is moving forward. Next stop, after the third preseason game where few 53-man roster players will participate, is the initial cutdown from 90 players. A lot has changed since our most recent 53-man roster projection , where we predicted Sanders would be traded after Watson got the starting job. A trade is still a possibility, even if unlikely, after the veteran got the nod from HC Todd Monken. DE Alex Wright is out for the season, with veteran DE Derek Barnett taking his spot , and we’ve seen some players seemingly secure their spot on the roster . Instead of creating our own 53-man projection, we are looking at the one put out by ESPN’s Daniel Oyefusi and evaluating what we see from that roster: Quarterbacks (4) Deshaun Watson, Shedeur Sanders, Dillon Gabriel, Taylen Green Keeping four quarterbacks seems like the likely decision at this point, as the three backups will likely get claimed by other teams. Cleveland can get creative by releasing a veteran on the last year of their deal, only to sign them a day later when they waive Green or Gabriel, trying to sneak them to the practice squad, but that is still risky. A trade is still in the cards, potentially. Running backs (4) Quinshon Judkins, Dylan Sampson, Raheim Sanders, Michael Burton (fullback) Keeping Burton, who hasn’t practiced at all in training camp, is an interesting decision over using a tight end like Ryan in the role while keeping Ahmani Marshall or another back for Monken’s run-heavy system. Tight ends (3) Harold Fannin Jr., Blake Whiteheart, Carsen Ryan No one knows for sure the status of Joe Royer , so GM Andrew Berry might be left with just three tight ends after Jack Stoll went on injured reserve. Among the weakest roster spots in Cleveland. Wide receivers (5) Jerry Jeudy, KC Concepcion, Denzel Boston, Isaiah Bond, Tylan Wallace Keeping “just” five receivers would be part of the issue with keeping four quarterbacks. Malachi Corley, Luke Floreia, Cedric Tillman, and Gage Larvadain all have reasons they could/should be the sixth receiver. Offensive linemen (10) Spencer Fano, Zion Johnson, Elgton Jenkins, Teven Jenkins, Tytus Howard, Dawand Jones, Parker Brailsford, Austin Barber, KT Leveston, Luke Wypler The same 10 linemen we projected before the first preseason game; the Browns roster has some depth here, but keeping three centers (E. Jenkins, Brailsford, Wypler) may not end up making sense. Defensive linemen (8) Jared Verse, Maliek Collins, Mason Graham, Isaiah McGuire, Derek Barnett, Mike Hall Jr., Adin Huntington, Kalia Davis Berry seems to be on the hunt for another defensive end, which could bump this number to nine. Logan Fano and Sam Kamara could make a case to make the roster as well. Some upfront talent, for sure, but a lot of depth concerns at this spot. Linebackers (6) Carson Schwesinger, Quincy Williams, Easton Mascarenas-Arnold, Winston Reid, Nathaniel Watson, Justin Jefferson It feels like a choice between a sixth linebacker (Watson, Reid, or EMA) versus keeping a fifth safety was made to favor the second level. Some tough decisions to be made. Cornerbacks (6) Denzel Ward, Tyson Campbell, Myles Harden, D’Angelo Ross, Tre Avery, Michael Coats Jr. Avery has looked a bit lost in coverage but has value on special teams, along with Ross. Trusting Coats then as the team’s fourth cornerback, potentially, could be risky, which is why DC Mike Rutenberg deploys three safeties quite often. Safeties (4) Grant Delpit, Ronnie Hickman, Emmanuel McNeil-Warren, Christopher Edmonds Edmonds is a bit of a surprise here, especially over McMillon. As noted, four safeties could be impacted by keeping six linebackers and four quarterbacks. Special teams (3) Andre Szmyt (K), Corey Bojorquez (P), Rex Sunahara (LS) Nailed it! What do you think about this projected 53-man roster? Where are the biggest misses? The weakest spots? The most depth? Join the conversation! title: How would you have handled the Browns starting QB decision?
summary: Head Coach Todd Monken announced that Deshaun Watson will start at quarterback in Week 1. It’s a controversial decision, especially after his poor performance in the second half of the preseason game against the Buffalo Bills and his comments during the postgame press conference. His criticism of the fans for booing is likely to make for […]
full_text: Head Coach Todd Monken announced that Deshaun Watson will start at quarterback in Week 1 . It’s a controversial decision, especially after his poor performance in the second half of the preseason game against the Buffalo Bills and his comments during the postgame press conference . His criticism of the fans for booing is likely to make for an even more hostile atmosphere when the Cleveland Browns return to Huntington Bank Field for their first home game in Week 3. Sources have said that the team went with Watson because of the experience he brings to the table compared to Shedeur Sanders . The coaching staff evaluated both quarterbacks throughout training camp and the first two preseason games and ultimately concluded that Watson is more ready. Earlier in the process, some believed Dillon Gabriel was making a push to join the competition , but that never came to fruition. Monken could have also waited longer to make the decision, giving each a quarter in the third preseason game. Instead, the Cleveland head coach gave the team three weeks to prepare for Week 1 with Watson. Watson has not played in a regular-season game since 2024 and is still working his way back from an Achilles injury, raising questions about whether he can keep pace with the speed of the game. Starting Sanders would have offered more upside, as he is only in the second year of his career and still has plenty of room to develop, while Watson’s play has declined significantly from the peak of his career. If Watson comes out slow against the Jacksonville Jaguars, the questions about this decision will only grow. Let me know what you think in the comments – How would you have handled the decision? title: 5 bubble guys fighting for a Cowboys roster spot
summary: The Dallas Cowboys will have some difficult decisions to make soon as final roster cuts approach, which means they’ll have to say goodbye to some of our fan favorites this year. There’s just no way to fit everyone, but who stays and who goes is heavily debated throughout August. With several players still having a […]
full_text: The Dallas Cowboys will have some difficult decisions to make soon as final roster cuts approach, which means they’ll have to say goodbye to some of our fan favorites this year. There’s just no way to fit everyone, but who stays and who goes is heavily debated throughout August. With several players still having a chance, we wanted to go through some of the top bubble guys and discuss how they got here and what they’ve done to put themselves in the running. Camden Brown An undrafted free agent from Georgia Southern, Brown didn’t make noise until his final year in college after spending his first three years at Auburn buried on the depth chart. A 65-catch, 1,079-yard season wasn’t enough to get drafted, but he’s taken full advantage of his opportunities in Dallas. His draft profile has been on full display in the preseason as his size and catch radius have helped him haul in everything thrown his way, dazzling fans with amazing catches against the Seahawks. But he also lacks breakaway speed, which kept him from turning on the jets and housing it on his long reception against the Cardinals. His first-team reps and unhideable highlights indicate the Cowboys either have to keep him or lose him, as his chances of clearing waivers and making it onto the practice squad are slim. How he makes it: He either beats out Jonathan Mingo or the team opts to keep six WRs. Julius Wood Third time’s a charm? Yes, this is the third chance with the Cowboys for the undrafted safety from East Carolina. Initially, signed as a priority free agent in 2024, Wood was thumping around at training camp to the point where many thought he would have made the team. He didn’t. The Titans claimed him, and he played nine games in his rookie season. He didn’t make Tennessee’s roster the following year, and this time it was the Cowboys who claimed him, where he stuck around on the practice squad all year last season. He signed a reserve/future deal in January, and he’s once again making his case to be on an NFL roster. He’s laying the smack and tackling everything, showcasing his high energy and physical playing style, but his lack of agility creates run-angle and coverage concerns that may not fit well with what the new coaching staff demands from the safety position. How he makes it: The team is deep this year at safety. They’d have to go extra long, especially considering how much they value Markquese Bell on special teams. Justin Barron After a five-year career at Syracuse trying to figure out what position fit him best, he finally settled in at linebacker. Average testing numbers resulted in him going undrafted, but he found a home with the Cowboys last year. He spent almost the entire year on the practice squad before being promoted for the final two games, where he played exclusively on special teams. He’s a smart player who processes fast and communicates well. It’s no surprise that he’s fitting in Christian Parker’s system, and he had himself quite the day with three interceptions in a scrimmage against the Rams. The question now becomes, can his noggin punch his ticket despite not having the strength or pure athleticism the position requires? How he makes it: He’s jumped veteran free agent signing Curtis Robinson, and the team only has four other linebackers ahead of him, so his chances are reasonable, but does the think they could be clever and try to sneak him on the practice squad? Reddy Steward With the Bears in 2024, UDFA Steward impressed in preseason, but didn’t make final roster cuts. He spent most of the year on their practice squad, only playing one game his rookie season. He signed a reserve/future deal with the Vikings last year, but again was waived at final roster cuts. The Cowboys immediately claimed him off waivers, where he played all 17 games last year. Steward has good instincts and solid run defender, which can keep him from giving up the big plays, but he allowed an 80% completion rate against him last season. He’s been doing well in camp, but the team’s slot corner options are far greater than they were a year ago. How me makes it: The team prefers its final corner spot to be used for the slot and not the boundary. Jay Toia When the Cowboys drafted the UCLA big man in the seventh round a year ago, their defensive tackle position group looked a lot different. They’ve since added Kenny Clark, Quinnen Williams, Otito Ogbannia, Jonathan Bullard, and LT Overton. This puts the 340-pound nose tackle in a tough spot. His brute strength and low center of gravity help him take on double teams and hold gaps, but his slow get-off and short arms keeps him from being a regular disruptor. He’s flashed some good play as of late, especially in the second preseason game against the Cardinals when he just blew up the interior, keeping him alive for one of those final roster spots. How he makes it: With three more years of team control, he still offers depth, and he could also get some help if the veteran Bullard starts the season on injured reserve.

summary: It is Day 19 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. full_text: UNITED STATES - JANUARY 04: Football: NFC championship, Dallas Cowboys Preston Pearson (26) in action, scoring TD vs Los Angeles Rams, Los Angeles, CA 1/4/1976 (Photo by Marvin E. Newman/Sports Illustrated via Getty Images) (SetNumber: X20155) It is Day 19 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like how big the game was for the organization, how memorable the game was, games that had unusual events take place, games that are a part of NFL lore, Cowboys firsts, and games where the Cowboys just plain dominated. Variety is the spice of life and we have all different kind of Cowboys games to review. At the bottom, we’ll link each day of the countdown so you can go back and check out any you missed. It’s now Day 19 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff, when we revisit one of the most dominant postseason performances of the Tom Landry era. One week after surviving Minnesota through the original Hail Mary, the Cowboys travelled to Los Angeles and overwhelmed the heavily favored Rams to capture the NFC championship and advance to Super Bowl X. Sunday, January 4, 1976 Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, Los Angeles, California Final Score: Dallas Cowboys 37, Los Angeles Rams 7 Dallas had missed the playoffs in 1974 and entered the 1975 postseason as a wild-card team after finishing 10-4. Los Angeles went 12-2, possessed the NFL’s top-ranked scoring and total defense, and had home-field advantage at the Coliseum. None of those advantages mattered once the Cowboys began turning Rams mistakes into points. The tone was established immediately. Linebacker D.D. Lewis intercepted James Harris’ first pass and gave Dallas possession inside Los Angeles territory. Roger Staubach capitalized by throwing an 18-yard screen pass to Preston Pearson for the opening touchdown. Staubach later found Golden Richards from four yards out, giving the Cowboys a 14-0 first-quarter lead. Dallas continued applying pressure before halftime. Pearson made a diving 15-yard touchdown reception for his second score of the afternoon, extending the lead to 21-0. Against a Rams defense that had been the league’s best throughout the regular season, the Cowboys had scored touchdowns on three of their most important early opportunities. Any possibility of a Los Angeles comeback disappeared after the break. Staubach used a shovel pass to Pearson for a 19-yard touchdown, giving Pearson three receiving scores and pushing the margin to 28-0. Toni Fritsch then converted field goals from 40 and 26 yards as Dallas built a remarkable 34-point advantage. The Rams finally reached the end zone during the fourth quarter when John Cappelletti scored on a one-yard run. Fritsch answered with another 26-yard field goal to complete the scoring. Los Angeles had entered expecting to represent the NFC in the Super Bowl, but Dallas never allowed the game to become competitive. This game belongs on the countdown because it captured Landry’s Cowboys operating at their most complete. Staubach controlled the game, Pearson supplied the explosive plays and the Doomsday Defense erased one of the NFC’s strongest teams. Dallas did not merely win a conference championship on the road, it dismantled the conference’s top seed by 30 points. #Cowboys vs #Rams 1976 NFC Championship Final Score: Dallas Cowboys 37, Los Angeles Rams 7 #DallasCowboys #NFL (📽️: @nfl ) pic.twitter.com/5Iz912YzAV — Mike Poland (@kenfigkowboy) August 25, 2026 Interesting Facts About the Game The win gave the Cowboys their third NFC championship and sent the franchise to its third Super Bowl appearance in six seasons. title: Why the Cowboys should be cautious about Javonte Williams’ 2026 workload
summary: To this point in the summer, there has been plenty of discussion regarding the Dallas Cowboys’ 2026 running back room. While the position group as a whole has stolen some headlines, much of the conversation has centered around which runner will serve as the backup to the newly re-signed Javonte Williams. At this point one […]
full_text: To this point in the summer, there has been plenty of discussion regarding the Dallas Cowboys’ 2026 running back room. While the position group as a whole has stolen some headlines, much of the conversation has centered around which runner will serve as the backup to the newly re-signed Javonte Williams. At this point one year ago, it would have been hard to imagine Williams being where he is today. When Dallas signed the former Denver Bronco to a one-year deal last season, some questioned if he would even finish the 2025 season as Dallas’ lead back. Fast forward to today, and the 26-year-old is not only firmly cemented as one of the Cowboys’ top offensive weapons, but is also fresh off signing a new three-year deal. Williams was undoubtedly one of the most productive running backs in all of football last season. The former second-round pick finished in the top 10 in rushing yards (1,201), 10+ yard runs (26), Yards After Contact (896), and YPA (4.8). Williams provided stability to a Cowboys’ running back room that desperately needed it, and his career year helped lead Dallas to finish top 10 in team rushing Y/A for the first time since 2021. While there is no denying how good Williams was last season, he did endure a heavy workload while doing so. For the first time in his five-year NFL career, Williams played 250+ SNPs (snaps lined up on the field on run plays) and recorded 250+ rushing attempts, via Pro Football Focus . His 278 SNPs and 252 rushing attempts were the 11th and 10th most of any running back in the league, respectively. This workload is not par for the course for the North Carolina product. After entering the league and starting 16 games back in 2021, injury issues and inconsistent play limited the runner to 54 and 166 offensive snaps in 2022 and 2024. Williams’ ACL tear in October of 2022 severely impacted his final two years in Denver, and he himself has admitted he did not feel fully back until last season in Dallas. While much of the conversation this summer has been about which runner will serve as Williams’ backup, there needs to be more focus on how the Cowboys can manage their starter’s workload this season. There is no denying that Williams was a very productive runner last year, but he played much better when he was fresh at the start of the year. In Dallas’ first 10 games of the regular season, Williams recorded 809 rushing yards, an average of 81 per game, to go with a very impressive 5.0 Y/A. In the final six games he played in, those numbers dropped to 392 rushing yards and a pedestrian 4.3 Y/A. Rushing success will always impact overall team success, but Williams’ individual performance played a large part in how Dallas played as a whole last year. When he recorded 85 or more rushing yards, the Cowboys were 5-1-1. When he went for 83 or fewer, Dallas was 2-7. It was evident in the final six games of the regular season that Williams’ increased workload impacted his ability to bring that early-season explosiveness week in and week out. This year, the Cowboys need to find a way to not let history repeat itself. Whether it’s Malik Davis, Jaydon Blue, Phil Mafah, or a runner from outside the organization, the Cowboys need to prioritize finding a runner capable of a 60/40 split on carries early in the regular season. Doing so would allow Dallas to hopefully have Williams healthy and at his best as they head into a potential postseason run. Who do you think will get the second-most carries at running back for the Cowboys in 2006?
