title: 2024 Cardinals defense: Jonathan Gannon’s most consistent season
summary: As I explored the data around new Green Bay Packers defensive coordinator Jonathan’s Gannon’s Cardinals defense, it appeared to me that 2024 was their most consistent year. Largely because they relied more on early down zone coverage for the entire year, unlike 2023. And if 2023 was about how much zone the Cardinals could run, […]
full_text: As I explored the data around new Green Bay Packers defensive coordinator Jonathan’s Gannon’s Cardinals defense, it appeared to me that 2024 was their most consistent year. Largely because they relied more on early down zone coverage for the entire year, unlike 2023. And if 2023 was about how much zone the Cardinals could run, 2024 was about how well they could sustain it. The defense pushed its early down zone rate to a three-year high of 43.36%, but the real story isn’t the number itself — it’s how little it moved. Early down coverage for Gannon’s Cardinals changed very little from the first half of the season to the second half of the season. In other words, whatever the Cardinals were doing in terms of early down coverage in the first half of the season, they basically continued to do in the second half of the season. This is in stark contrast to 2023 when the staff basically overhauled the coverage shell from the first half of the season to the second half of the season. The Early Down Identity: Zone-First, Refined The defense was in zone coverage on 43.36% of early down plays (379 plays) in 2024. Man coverage was used on just 9.61% of early down plays (84 plays) in 2024. Thus, the 2024 Cardinals were in zone coverage on 4.5 times as many early down plays as they were in man coverage. This makes the 2024 Cardinals the most zone-tilted defense in the three years of data in the sample. Again, referencing the Early Down sections above, it is noted that within coverage shells the Cardinals used most early down plays in Cover 3 (20.71% or +9.7% over 2023 levels of 18.87% or 166 plays of early down coverage). Next for the Cardinals in terms of early down zone coverage were plays in which they employed a Cover 4 look (13.16% or 115 plays of early down zone coverage in 2024 that were classified as Cover 4, +0% over 2023 levels of 13.08% or 116 plays of early down coverage in 2018 that were classified as Cover 4). Finally, as noted above in the Man Coverage section, early down Man Coverage for the Cardinals in 2024 consisted of plays in which the team employed a Cover 1 look (7.21% or 63 plays of early down Man Coverage in 2024, down from 8.09% or 72 plays in 2023 of early down coverage in which the Cardinals used a Cover 1 look for Man Coverage). Overall, the Cardinals used less Man Coverage in 2024 than in 2023. Here’s a look at how the 3-safety disguise pre-snap turns into cover-3 post snap for each of those coverages. Within their zone coverage package, Gannon found creative ways to sustain their trends. The use of a 3-high safety defense pre-snap allowed them to rotate to other zone coverages in non-traditional ways, coverages like cover-3, Tampa-2, and cover-6. The usage of Cover 6 increased to 5.95% (52 plays) of the total early down plays in 2024. This was an increase from the 4.96% (46 plays) of early down plays in 2023. This increase shows that the coaching staff was trying out a variety of different split field packages to see if any of them would work. Cover 2 Man was used only once the entire season at 0.11%. This would indicate that the staff saw little to no value in using this package, and thus used it very sparingly as a novelty package. First Half to Second Half: Remarkable Stability As opposed to 2023 where the early down identity of the Cardinals’ defense went through drastic in-season changes (e.g. shifting from a Cover 3-based identity to a Cover 4-based identity), 2024 saw the early down identity of the Cardinals’ defense remain relatively stable from start to finish. Instead of seeing dramatic fluctuations in early down coverage, early down zone-coverage rates remained relatively stable, decreasing by only 1.3% throughout the season. This level of stability within the core coverage shells, when translated into scheme-level usage, shows how the staff found increased success with a variety of live and creative packages, including a remarkable late season uptick in early down blitzing with Cover 0 (which rose 34.6% from 2.05% to 2.76% for the season). Similarly, the split-field package of Cover 6 saw increased usage, up 9.5% from 5.68% to 6.22% for the season. Third Down: Peak Aggression, Balanced Approach On third down the Cardinals ran the most zone coverage of any season in the sample, and at the same time saw the highest rate of man coverage on third down of the last three years. The 20.22% early down blitz rate on third down looked to match the team’s 20.91% early down blitz rate from 2023 on early downs. This would suggest that the team is able to bring a number of different live answers to third down situations. The Cardinals used slightly more everything on third down in 2024 than in 2023. For one, the defense used more zone on third down in 2024 than in 2023. The Cardinals used zone on 48.69% of third downs in 2024, up from 44.44% in 2023. The Cardinals used more man coverage on third down in 2024 than in 2023, but not as much as the increase in zone. Finally, the Cardinals used more blitzes on third down in 2024 than in 2023. Third Down Stability Third Down is very similar from the first half to the second half of the season. Man coverage is down 5.8% from 20.45% to 19.26%, while Zone coverage is up 0.8% from 48.48% to 48.89%. The defense’s Blitz rate on third down is down 9.2% from 21.21% to 19.26%. 2023 to 2024: What Actually Changed The changes in usage between 2023 and 2024 for each of the different schemes can be seen in the graph above. The largest increases in usage for the biggest schemes of coverage were for Cover 3, which increased by the largest margin (+9.7%), and for Cover 6, which increased to a large degree (+20.0%). There were moderate increases in usage for Cover 0 and for Cover 2. The largest decreases in usage for the biggest schemes of coverage were for Cover 4, which decreased by -4.4%, and for Cover 1, which decreased by -10.9%. This would indicate that the Cardinals’ staff trimmed the secondary zone looks and the team’s primary man coverage in order to add to the other looks. It’s hard to know for sure why the 2024 Cardinals are better than the 2023 version of the team. The team has clearly solved their personnel problems. Whether that’s through free agency, the draft or just having a full off-season to get a scheme to work for them rather than trying to tweak things on the fly like they did in 2023 is impossible to know for sure. Key Takeaways Most Zone-Tilted Season in Sample. The 2024 defense was the most zone-tilted of the three-year sample. The early down identity featured a 4.5-to-1 ratio of early down plays in zone coverage (43.36% of 874 plays; 379 plays total) to early down plays in man coverage (9.61% of 874 plays; 84 plays total). As noted above, the most played coverage shell was Cover 3, the Cardinals’ base zone package. Cover 3 was the most played coverage shell in the sample for the 2024 defense. Specifically, the base zone package was played on 20.71% of the total early down plays in the sample for 2024 (or 181 of 874 total early down plays in the sample for 2024). This total for Cover 3 represented a large increase from 2023, where the base Cover 3 package was played on 18.87% of the early down plays in the sample for 2023 (or 164 of 868 early down plays in the sample for 2023; 18.87% – 9.7% = 9.17%). The team’s other primary early down zone package, Cover 4, was played on 13.16% of the early down plays in the sample for 2024 (or 115 of the 874 early down plays in the sample for 2024). Stability instead of Change. In the section Early Down Identity: Zone-First, Refined for the section The Early Down Identity: Zone-First, Refined on page 6 of the Cardinals 2024 Season Review, Early Down Coverage by First Half and Season was graphed. The graph for the first half of season and for the whole season for each of the three coverage shells was almost identical. In other words, the Cardinals did not change their early down coverage as much as they changed it in the second half of the 2023…

title: Aaron Banks, the Packers, and the sunk cost fallacy
summary: The Cleveland Browns and their years-long saga with Deshaun Watson has brought up a lot of arguments citing the “sunk cost fallacy” as to why the Browns should stop considering their quarterback’s hefty contract when making decisions about their future. The Green Bay Packers might already have a similar (albeit less impactful) situation on their […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MN - JANUARY 04: Green Bay Packers guard Aaron Banks (65) looks on before the NFL game between the Green Bay Packers and Minnesota Vikings on January 4th, 2026, at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis, MN. (Photo by Bailey Hillesheim/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Cleveland Browns and their years-long saga with Deshaun Watson has brought up a lot of arguments citing the “ sunk cost fallacy ” as to why the Browns should stop considering their quarterback’s hefty contract when making decisions about their future. The Green Bay Packers might already have a similar (albeit less impactful) situation on their hands with offensive guard Aaron Banks. Last offseason, the Packers made some surprising free agent acquisitions, most notably with Banks, to whom they gave a four-year, $77 million deal . That was a hefty price tag on an offensive guard who struggled with consistency during his time with the San Francisco 49ers, and a lot of those same issues popped up in his first season with the Packers. According to Pro Football Focus , Banks allowed two sacks and 27 pressures in on 484 pass-blocking snaps last season. That’s not ideal for a player who is the NFL’s seventh-highest paid left guard by average annual salary. For reference, here’s how the other highest-paid left guards fared in pass protection. Peter Skoronski ($25 million AAV): two sacks, 23 pressures (694 pass-blocking snaps) Tyler Smith ($24 million): three sacks, 26 pressures (700 snaps) Matthew Bergeron ($23.5 million): one sack, 28 pressures (519 snaps) Luke Goedeke ($22.5 million): zero sacks, 22 pressures (416 snaps) Landon Dickerson ($21 million): five sacks, 33 pressures (506 snaps) Quenton Nelson ($20 million): one sack, 15 pressures (637 snaps) Aaron Banks ($19.25 million): two sacks, 27 pressures (484 snaps) Joe Thuney ($17.5 million): zero sacks, 22 pressures (788 snaps) Zion Johnson ($16.5 million): five sacks, 29 pressures (708 snaps) David Edwards ($15.25 million): four sacks, 32 pressures (679 snaps) Note that while some of these names have similar sack/pressure numbers to Banks, they also played significantly more snaps than the Packers iOL did last season. The only name who had similar struggles with a similar snap count was Landon Dickerson during a tumultuous offensive season with the Philadelphia Eagles. The worry is that because of Banks’ large contract, the Packers might be eager to prove themselves right by trying to continue leaning on him as a full-time starter to justify the deal. But the Packers have other options to potentially replace a struggling Banks, most notably in fifth-round rookie Jager Burton, who has shown some legitimate flashes this preseason to potentially earn a starting job. Other options are also on the tape, including Anthony Belton and Jacob Monk, although one of those three options will likely be slotting into the other guard spot opposite of Banks. The good news is that the Packers already have a recent track record of not falling into the sunk-cost trap. Cornerback Nate Hobbs was Green Bay’s other splash free-agent signing last offseason, signing a four-year, $48 million deal. After a disappointing year, the Packers decided to cut ties with Hobbs and eat the dead cap money rather than trying to force a fit that wasn’t working. There’s a chance the Packers could make a similar decision next offseason with Banks if he continues to disappoint. And as of right now, the signs aren’t looking good for Banks, who has missed a big portion of training camp while dealing with knee tendinitis . While the Packers continue to support Banks, frustration has started to slip out with the coaching staff about their guard’s availability. Earlier in camp, head coach Matt LaFleur praised Burton and Monk for performing well in practices, but appeared frustrated when mentioning Banks’ availability. #Packers Matt LaFleur was candid on if Aaron Banks will get his LG position back when he's healthy? Jager Burton and Jacob Monk are making it hard. "He (Banks) hasn't been out there so it's hard to say." #GoPackGo pic.twitter.com/2KEImJteRk — Vince Lovergine (@Vince_Lovergine) August 15, 2026 Time will tell how the Packers handle the left guard spot, but if Banks is able to play and struggles early, his contract can’t be a part of the team’s decision on whether to play someone else.

title: Green Bay Packers News: Cardinals arrive for joint practices
summary: Now that the long-threatened and long-feared Rivalries uniforms have been revealed, all that’s left between the Packers’ and the regular season is a week of practices with the Cardinals and one last exhibition game. title: Packers unveil new ‘Rivalries’ uniform
summary: The Packers have unveiled their new “Rivalries” uniforms, and they confirm what we’ve previously suspected: the uniforms pay tribute to the Packers’ unique ownership structure, and Ed Policy was absolutely right in his extremely tepid praise for them. These are certainly among the Packers’ uniforms of all time. The set trades the Packers’ iconic green […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - AUGUST 16: An overview of a Green Bay Packers logo on the side of a helmet as it sits on the field before the NFL preseason game between the Green Bay Packers and the Indianapolis Colts on August 16, 2025, at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Allio/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Packers have unveiled their new “Rivalries” uniforms, and they confirm what we’ve previously suspected: the uniforms pay tribute to the Packers’ unique ownership structure, and Ed Policy was absolutely right in his extremely tepid praise for them. These are certainly among the Packers’ uniforms of all time. The set trades the Packers’ iconic green and gold for a pair of colors Nike is calling “vintage green” and “alabaster,” which basically look like washed out versions of green and gold. Not exactly the strongest start if you’re trying to represent the essence of the Packers, but we can work with it if we have to, I guess. The rest of the storytelling elements (and there are always storytelling elements, it’s never just a uniform, even if it’s a transparently cynical merchandising cash grab) point basically in the direction we expected. Ed Policy said last year that the uniforms were inspired by “one of the most unique and defining pieces of Packers history” and that they would “celebrate owners.” I don’t know if you can call this, at best, pretty “meh” uniform a celebration of anything other than the money it will generate in jersey sales, but Nike is certainly trying to tell the story of the Packers’ ownership. As I predicted last week , the Packers’ new uniforms pay homage to the Packers’ shareholder certificates, both in their color scheme and in the numerals. The colors, Nike says in the official reveal , are “reminiscent of the aged paper color of historic Packers stock certificates and accented with the team’s signature gold.” The numbers, meanwhile, are intended to call to mind “the intricate lettering on paper currency, reflective of the financial contributions from the fans that helped sustain the franchise over the years.” You can also see a different font on the lettering used on the nameplate . The Packers’ helmet is reminiscent of their “Winter Warning” alternate at first glance, but there are a few changes. The new look has a green facemask and lacks the small green and gold flecks in the finish. It also has an interlocking GB logo on the back, and the helmet stripe has some texturing/detailing on it that Nike says is supposed to echo “the ornate borders found on Packers stock certificates.” There’s also similar detailing on the numbers. The jersey also features the Packers’ little-used interlocking GB logo, something Vince Lombardi tried to popularize during his reign as the Packers’ head coach, which you can see on this famous picture of the coach . All that is fine, in its own way, but I think we are obligated to talk about the larger universe in which these uniforms exist. I know they’re not for me. Maybe they’re not for you. I’ve said previously (somewhat but not entirely tongue in cheek) that this whole “Rivalries” uniforms push exists only to appease an extremely online group of fans, all of them younger than me, who tend to describe uniforms in terms of how “clean” or “fire” (or fire emoji) they may be, and I still understand that to be true. Whatever my taste may be, these uniforms are not intended for me. I’m already in the ecosystem. They’re not trying to court my attention or bring me into the tent as a long-term consumer of NFL goods and media. And to the extent that I want more people to be fans of football because I think it’s a good and worthwhile thing to follow, I’m fine with that. If these uniforms convert a few more people into Packers fans, I can be okay with that — to a point. But. The Packers are one of the oldest and (not using this term lightly) most iconic franchises in the NFL. Their story is one of independence and self-determination. They exist in the world of big money professional sports not because of their deep-pocketed owner, but in spite of the fact that they don’t have one at all. A megacorporation like Nike hijacking their visual identity to sell some more consumer goods is antithetical to that story, no matter how many nods they make to the people who actually own the Packers. And a hijacking is exactly what it is. This is not a uniform the Packers would have chosen for themselves. They already have one of the most recognizable uniforms in sports. They categorically do not need any help. The green and gold. The white block lettering. The G itself. Those elements already tell the story of the Packers, and that story doesn’t need a reinterpretation or reimagining. It’s already fine as is. Way better than fine, in fact. It’s easy to dismiss it as “just a uniform,” but it’s not just a uniform. It’s a conscious choice to take control of the Packers’ story, and if the Packers’ story is about ownership, this is an affront to that story. They’ll wear this “Rivalry” uniform in Week 5 against the Bears, their oldest and most hated rival, but if I can do a little marketing storytelling myself, maybe this whole thing shows us who their real rivals should be. It’s not the Bears. It’s the people who want the Packers to be just like every other team.
author: Jon Meerdink

title: Value of Things: Nick Caserio growing in the job
summary: There are three things that people know about me if they are regular readers of this feature. These three things intersect here in one spot, so I thought it was a good time to talk about them for those that are joining us for the first time. The first thing is that writing is not […]
full_text: There are three things that people know about me if they are regular readers of this feature. These three things intersect here in one spot, so I thought it was a good time to talk about them for those that are joining us for the first time. The first thing is that writing is not actually my day job. I am a teacher and I could go into specifics, but I generally support special education students in English classes. Someone somewhere decided that I could write a little and therefore I could be helpful there. It’s a crazy notion. The second fact is that I also write for our sister site “The Crawfish Boxes” and baseball is probably my first love. I have been doing baseball numbers for decades now and decided to pour that love (the third thing about me) into this feature on Battle Red Blog. All three of these things intersect today as I will describe shortly. In teaching, they taught us the trick that we affectionately call the sandwich. When you are doing a parent/teacher conference it is almost always because there is a problem. Parents are naturally defensive when there is a problem and meetings can get off to a contentious start. So, we do something called the sandwich. We start with a positive about the student, follow it with the problem, and then end with another positive. This puts the parent at ease and also gives them a positive taste in their mouth when the meeting ends. We are much more likely to get buy in when we do things that way. Commentary by its very nature is a critical thing. It’s not a ton of fun to use numbers and analytical analysis to talk about how good something is. Some of us here are more positive than others, but I recognize that I tend to fall on the realistic/pessimistic end of that continuum. So, when we are looking at guys like Nick Caserio and DeMeco Ryans, it is easy to get stuck in a loop of constantly criticizing facets of their performance that we find lacking. Positivity simply doesn’t sell. This is where the baseball portion of the equation fits in. The Houston Astros just dismissed their general manager. We could get into the weeds (and I have at Crawfish) but he was essentially let go because of excessive inaction. He let problems fester either because he was unwilling or unable to fix them. I don’t write about the Houston Rockets, but we could say something similar about Rafael Stone. That should highlight the difference between Caserio and the other two decision makers in Houston. We could say a lot about why the Texans felt the need to add three wide receivers in a week. We could say a lot about who he decided to add and the price he paid. I think we can grossly simply it by saying that he and the coaching staff were not satisfied with the wide receiver even independent of the Jayden Higgins injury. It is certainly fair to speculate about who they are unsatisfied with. I could imagine that maybe Tank Dell is not going to be ready at the opening bell. The same could be true of Jaylin Noel. We could also look at the likelihood that veterans like Justin Watson and Xavier Hutchinson are deemed as just not good enough. I’m not going to put words in the mouth of the coaching staff. They can certainly speak for themselves and I imagine how they set up their 53 man roster and injured reserve will speak volumes. However, this is how organizations are supposed to work. The coaching staff communicates a need and the front office works quickly to find a solution. Are any of these three good solutions? We honestly won’t know until we see it (or don’t see it) on the field. Decisive action is not necessarily the same thing as wise action, but it is certainly preferrable to no action at all. Certainly, when you look at the comments here and at other Texans’ fan sites you can see the criticism. Most of it involves how the offensive line is built. There is certainly more than enough there to chew on. However, I am using my teacher method here and sandwiching that criticism with some positives. The main positive is decisive action. Caserio moves quickly to solve problems. He generally does not hold onto mistakes forever. Most people can identify when they have screwed up. Most people also find ways to deflect and make excuses for those mistakes. He largely has not done that. So, I offer this as the first half of a sandwich for the criticism I know is coming. I may very well end up panning these additions if they don’t perform on the field. I appreciate the effort though. I appreciate actually addressing a problem in real time. It recognizes the urgency of the situation. It not only addresses the wide receiver room itself, but also the idea that this team has a tighter championship window than they have had the last couple of years. So, kudos to Caserio for now. Obviously stay tuned to see if it all works out.

title: Houston Texans 53-man roster prediction post-Boutte trade
summary: This is the second-to-last Rosterology before the 53-man roster cut down. There has been a TON of roster movement over the past 72 hours which has impacted the Rosterology in an immense way. This is easily the most unsettled a Texans roster has been heading into the final preseason game in quite a while. The […]
full_text: Houston Texans players celebrate an 80-yard interception return for a touchdown by Houston Texans linebacker Wade Woodaz during the first half of an NFL preseason football game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Reliant Stadium in Houston, Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026. (Photo by Brett Coomer/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images) This is the second-to-last Rosterology before the 53-man roster cut down. There has been a TON of roster movement over the past 72 hours which has impacted the Rosterology in an immense way. This is easily the most unsettled a Texans roster has been heading into the final preseason game in quite a while. The linebackers are a mess. Who is our RB3? What is Tank Dell’s timeline? Are the Texans bad or simply not deep? Injuries : DE Dylan Horton, WR Jayden Higgins, RB Joshua Pitsenberger, WR Montrell Washington, LB K.C. Ossai, WR D.J. Turner Additions : WR Kayshon Boutte, WR Zay Jones, QB Brett Rypien, WR Sterling Shepard, RB Owen Wright, LB Caleb Johnson, CB Bryce Hall, CB George Odum Cuts : LB Marte Mapu (injury), LB Sione TakiTaki Traded Away : S Jaylen Reed Here are the past 53-man roster predictions Rosterology 1.0 Rosterology 2.0 Rosterology 3.0 Note: Rookies are in bold , UDFAs are italicized , and new players are in *asterisks* Last Four In: Justin Watson, WR Aiden Fisher, LB Noah Whittington, RB Solomon Byrd, DE First Four Out: Sterling Shepard, WR Jake Andrews, OC Naquan Jones, DT Collin Wright, CB Biggest Riser: Noah Whittington, RB Whittington has been the only positive on the offense all preseason. He’s a gritty runner whose health has been his biggest asset. He of course suffered an ankle injury during the game, but it’s yet to be see how severe an injury. He should get the nod on the roster and threaten Jawhar Jordan’s spot. Biggest Faller: Jared Wayne, WR Before, the preseason game against the Raiders, Wayne was having a coming-out party at camp. After the flurry of WR additions, there’s no possible avenue for him to make the 53. He’s ascended throughout camp, that’s for sure, but he couldn’t shine in either preseason game and wasn’t enough to stymie GM Nick Caserio from bringing in multiple options at WR. Offense (26) Quarterbacks: 2 C.J. Stroud, Davis Mills CUT: *Brett Rypien* Analysis: Mertz’ injury was a rough watch, but somehow equally rough was watching QB Brett Rypien try to play football. There’s no way he deserves a roster spot after his brutal performance. His inability to run the offense, lack of pocket awareness, and multiple fumbles directly led to the Raiders comeback win in the preseason game. Less than half of the league will keep only two QBs. The Texans should be one of those teams this year. Running Backs: 5 David Montgomery, Woody Marks, Jawhar Jordan, British Brooks, Noah Whittington CUT: *Deuce Vaughn*, *Owen Wright* INJURED RESERVE: Joshua Pitsenberger Analysis: Houston have kept five RBs each of the past three seasons. I project them to do the same this year too. British Brooks’ returned yesterday from a broken hand. Any further delay would have landed him on IR. He needs to get significant snaps in the last preseason game to secure his spot. Noah Whittington has earned a roster spot. Injured Jawhar Jordan hasn’t proven enough to hold down the RB3 spot without question. Even so, the team likes him enough to keep him around and have not designated him for IR yet. Wide Receivers: 6 Nico Collins, Justin Watson, Xavier Hutchinson, Lewis Bond , Jaylin Noel, Kayshon Bouttee CUT: Jared Wayne, Daniel Sobkowics, Treyvhon Saunders, Jha’Quan Jackson, Juwann Winfree, *Zay Jones*, *Sterling Shepard* INJURED RESERVE: Jayden Higgins, Tank Dell, DJ Turner Analysis: Complete overhaul is an understatement. Losing Higgins for the year is a huge blow. It sparked a classic Caserio shopping spree where he acquired Zay Jones, Sterling Shepard, and Kayshon Boutte. It’s a complete unknown how the team values Shepard and Jones over Justin Watson and Jared Wayne. Bond should be a lock even with the changes. Noel returns to the roster after recovering from his pinkie injury. Tight Ends: 4 Dalton Schultz, Marlin Klein , Foster Moreau, Cade Stover CUT: Brevin Jordan, Layne Pryor, Louis Hansen Analysis: Brevin Jordan has been sidelined for weeks due to a knee injury. His time in Houston has to be over. Stover has played well, earned a spot, and carved a roll out at fullback too. Offensive Lineman: 9 Aireontae Ersery, Braden Smith, Trent Brown, Wyatt Teller, Blake Fisher, Keylan Rutledge, Febechi Nwaiwu , Ed Ingram, Evan Brown CUT: Jake Andrews, Jarrett Patterson, Eli Cox, Jarrett Kingston, Sam Hagen, James Neal III Analysis: Welcome back, Evan Brown. He started the preseason game at center. Blake Fisher has looked next to horrible in preseason contests. He could… and honestly should be a roster casualty. He’s an extremely cheap break glass option and probably would get picked up by another squad if he’s released. Jarrett Patterson is an irrelevant piece of the puzzle at this junction. He’s lost out to Brown and Andrews, let alone Nwaiwu and Rutledge. Defense (24) Defensive Ends: 4 Will Anderson Jr., Danielle Hunter, Dylan Horton, Jadeveon Clowney, Solomon Byrd CUT: Dominique Robinson, Ali Gaye, Sabastian Harsh INJURED RESERVE: Dylan Horton Analysis: Distraught isn’t a poignant enough word to describe the feeling of hearing Horton’s achilles injury. He’s entering a contract year and was in line for a major backup role on the defense. He’s replaced by Solomon Byrd, whose impressive tackles for loss were offset by his inability to set the edge against the run. It’s rare to say a player is trying too hard, but that’s the case with Byrd. Dominique Robinson is dealing with a calf injury, which thins this DE room out considerably. Too bad Derek Barnett signed with the Cleveland Browns one day ago – he could have been a Texan again. Houston could be in the market for a DE after roster cutdowns. Defensive Tackles: 5 Tommy Togiai, Sheldon Rankins, Kayden McDonald , Logan Hall, Mario Edwards Jr. CUT: Naquan Jones, Dominic Bailey, Kyonte Hamilton Analysis: The main update is swapping Mario Edwards Jr. for Naquan Jones. Jones has been given every opportunity to succeed, but has not raised any provocation to earn a roster spot. I personally would keep Jones and his youth over Edwards, but they must believe they can stash Jones on the practice squad again. Linebackers: 6 Henry To’oTo’o, Azeez Al-Shaair, Wade Woodaz , Jake Hummel, Jamal Hill, Aiden Fisher INJURED RESERVE: E.J. Speed, Jake Hansen CUT: K.C. Ossai, Marte Mapu (injury), *Caleb Johnson* Analysis: The LBs went from the deepest to the thinnest room in three weeks. Mapu is out. Woodaz broke his thumb but should be cleared for Week One. Hummel looks competent but slow. Jamal Hill looks lost on defense. The rookie Aiden Fisher has outplayed almost every other backup LB on the roster. He will be a special teams contributor. The Texans need Jake Hansen back urgently. He was seen running at practice but not participating in drills. Cornerbacks: 5 Derek Stingley Jr., Kamari Lassiter, Jaylin Smith, Alijah Huzzie, Tremon Smith CUT: Collin Wright , Ja’Marcus Ingram, Brandon Codrington, Stephen Hall , Bryce Hall Analysis: Veteran Tremon Smith has been running with the third-string CBs, which is not a good sign for him. Collin Wright is still recovering from a soft tissue injury and has missed the past week-plus of camp. I think they trust Huzzie a lot at corner even if he hasn’t played miraculously well in preseason. Until Wright is fully healthy, he’s behind Smith and Huzzie on the depth chart. Safeties: 4 Reed Blankenship, Calen Bullock, Jalen Pitre, Kamari Ramsey CUT: Kevon Merriweather, *George Odum* INJURED RESERVE: M.J. Stewart Analysis: Film review illustrated Jaylen Reed was not breaking well on routes, which led to a ton of big plays by opposing offenses in preseason. Trading him to the Patriots was NOT on my bingo card, but it shows how much depth the team has at safety. Rookie…

title: Did Disney drop the ball on choice of obscure character for Colts apparel collaboration?
summary: On Monday, Disney and the NFL announced a collaboration for team-branded apparel, in which specific Disney characters would ‘join forces’ with each individual league team. Here’s a full list. For Horseshoe fans, it was the initial anticipation of getting to see which Disney, Pixar, Marvel, or Star Wars character would be aligned with their favorite […]
full_text: Anaheim, CA - January 23: Horace Horsecollar during Disney California Adventure's Lunar New Year celebration in Anaheim, CA, on Friday, January 23, 2026. They are celebrating The Year of the Horse January 23 through February 22, 2026. (Photo by Jeff Gritchen/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images) | MediaNews Group via Getty Images On Monday, Disney and the NFL announced a collaboration for team-branded apparel, in which specific Disney characters would ‘join forces’ with each individual league team. Here’s a full list . For Horseshoe fans, it was the initial anticipation of getting to see which Disney, Pixar, Marvel, or Star Wars character would be aligned with their favorite team, the Colts, for the 2026 campaign regarding the newly unveiled unique team apparel collaboration. Upon initial thought, there were a handful of popular Disney or Pixar horse characters that one would reasonably think would’ve been appropriate for the Colts to tag-team with—just to name a few: Bullseye (Toy Story) Maximus (Tangled) Pegasus (Hercules) Instead, Disney inexplicably chose an obscure old-time character, “Horace Horsecollar,” who debuted as Mickey’s plow horse back in 1929, as one of his oldest friends, and frequently appeared in Disney cartoons from 1930-32 before making his last appearance in the original Disney shorts in 1942. The Colts/Disney collab… pic.twitter.com/IqeY5tN8lB — ColtsFanCole (@ColtsFanCole) August 24, 2026 Horace would later make cameo character appearances in a few Disney films through the 1980’s and 1990’s, before later making appearances in the Mickey Mouse television series (2013) and most recently, Mickey Clubhouse+. Look, I can certainly appreciate the history of Horace Horsecollar, but how did the Los Angeles Chargers, whose emblem is a lightning bold, end up with BOTH Hercules AND Pegasus, when Hercules’ Zeus, Cars’ Lightning McQueen, or even The Incredibles’ super-villian Syndrome (who I believe utilized blue energy beams) all seem like more appropriate options, especially at the expense of the Colts losing a popular Disney/Pixar horse option. For what it’s worth, Maximus was chosen for the Denver Broncos which has already sold out among their fans on the official Disney store, and it’s hard to disagree with that selection given that like the Colts, they’re also purely a horse. Kudos to the Broncos for landing a good one! However, the Dallas Cowboys got both Toy Story’s Woody and Bullseye ( which also sold out respectively ), while the Houston Texans got Jessie and Bullseye ( *also sold out by the same token ). Could the Colts not have just gotten Bullseye by himself? We would’ve gladly taken it. I mean our rival Tennessee Titans got Thanos for gods’ sakes! At any rate, Horace Horsecollar it is, and if that’s not synonymous for the lost decade plus that’s been Colts football, having had prior glory years to fondly reminisce of, but currently floating in relative obscurity, then I don’t know what is.

title: Colts looked rough in their second preseason game
summary: Sometimes, a little bit of time and distance can make things that initially seemed terrible seem less so. Time heals all wounds, right? Yes, it’s just the preseason. No, it doesn’t count for anything. Yes, the Lions went 4-0 in the preseason before their 0-16 season. All of that is true. It is also true […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - AUGUST 22: Riley Leonard #15 of the Indianapolis Colts looks for a pass during a preseason game against the Atlanta Falcons at Lucas Oil Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Chris Carter/Getty Images) | Getty Images Sometimes, a little bit of time and distance can make things that initially seemed terrible seem less so. Time heals all wounds, right? Yes, it’s just the preseason. No, it doesn’t count for anything. Yes, the Lions went 4-0 in the preseason before their 0-16 season. All of that is true. It is also true that, no matter the circumstances, the Indianapolis Colts looked rough. If you had told me there was a quarterback battle, I would have thought the winner had to go fight a dragon because it seemed like neither man wanted the job. It didn’t help that the offensive line was a sieve and receivers had balls bouncing off their chests. Neither Riley Leonard nor Anthony Richardson looked comfortable at all against the Falcons’ second and third units, respectively. The only person who looked like they were on track for a roster spot was Deion Burks, who is making plays and using the return game to solidify his position. Speaking of roster spots, does Mekhi Blackmon have a spot on this team? That man is going to have a new nickname, Mr. Yellow, because that is all we see when he’s out there. He has to get the penalties down, or his spot with the Colts is gone. On top of that, the rest of the defense got little to no push or pressure. It looked like the Falcons’ offense was wearing the red quarterback non-contact jerseys the way they went untouched at times. Once again, there was a bright spot, as some of the rookies and linebackers did stand out. It wasn’t all bad, but it was tough to watch. So, did the game count? Nope. It will be a blip even on the Colts’ 2026 season, let alone historically. Did it count for guys trying to make the roster? It meant everything. A game like that was a collective effort and won’t undo all the positives a player has put together over training camp, but it doesn’t help. That’s why they play preseason games, well, that and money, but it’s a chance to show what one can do against true competition. It’s just preseason, but there isn’t enough time or space to make that one look pretty.
author: Jon Spradley

title: Can Anthony Richardson beat out Riley Leonard to be the Colts backup quarterback?
summary: Left for dead, Anthony Richardson’s career was on life support. For all intents and purposes it seemed that his days in the NFL were numbered and completely done as quarterback of the Indianapolis Colts. Things aren’t settled yet, but there is a legitimate chance Richardson is not only on the roster come Week 1, he […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - AUGUST 22: Wanya Morris #79 of the Atlanta Falcons tackles Anthony Richardson Sr. #5 of the Indianapolis Colts during the preseason game at Lucas Oil Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Chris Carter/Getty Images) | Getty Images Left for dead, Anthony Richardson’s career was on life support. For all intents and purposes it seemed that his days in the NFL were numbered and completely done as quarterback of the Indianapolis Colts. Things aren’t settled yet, but there is a legitimate chance Richardson is not only on the roster come Week 1, he could be QB2. After Riley Leonard impressed in Week 18 against Houston and fans witnessed an offseason of Richardson and the Colts looking for a trade partner, the odds were high that he would never take another snap for the horseshoe. He still may not take an official snap for the Colts, but Richardson is doing his best to make the Colts reconsider sending him on his way. Ed Dobbs already said the Colts will most likely retain him, but being the first backup was always the goal for Richardson in 2026. The starting role is gone, at least for now. Daniel Jones struggles to make it through a season unscathed. Enter Richardson. If he can beat out Leonard and gain that second slot, the improbable becomes reality. He isn’t there quite yet. A strong outing against the Patriots gave him signs of life. The Falcons’ game proved to be a step back, but Leonard looked no better. If Leonard continues to look less than stellar and Richardson regains his preseason game one form, he will be one injury away from potential redemption. There are a lot of ifs in the above. A lot has to go right for Anthony Richardson and a few things have to go wrong for others. It isn’t out of the realm of possibility, though. He still needs to show he is worthy of the backup spot by putting Saturday’s game behind him and turning in quality work going forward. Then, if given a chance, he can’t botch it. This may be the last chance he gets to resurrect his career. Fail to strike when opportunity comes his way and the plug on his NFL days will be pulled.

title: Colts Shane Steichen outlines playing time plan for preseason finale against Lions
summary: According to head coach Shane Steichen, the Indianapolis Colts starters will play roughly two series at home against the Detroit Lions on Saturday afternoon for the team’s preseason finale—although neither starting quarterback Daniel Jones nor running back Jonathan Taylor will play (via FOX59/CBS4’s Mike Chappell): Also of interesting note, is that Colts backup quarterback Anthony […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 7: Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts hands off to Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts during the NFL 2025 game between Miami Dolphins and Indianapolis Colts at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 7, 2025 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Hickey/Getty Images) | Getty Images According to head coach Shane Steichen, the Indianapolis Colts starters will play roughly two series at home against the Detroit Lions on Saturday afternoon for the team’s preseason finale—although neither starting quarterback Daniel Jones nor running back Jonathan Taylor will play (via FOX59/CBS4’s Mike Chappell): Colts starters will play 8-10 plays, two series. Daniel Jones and Jonathan Taylor will not play. Anthony Richardson Sr. will start vs. Lions. — Mike Chappell (@mchappell51) August 25, 2026 Also of interesting note, is that Colts backup quarterback Anthony Richardson Sr., who’s arguably outplayed challenger 2nd-year quarterback Riley Leonard for the team’s QB2 job behind Jones through two preseason games, will draw the start instead. Given Leonard’s struggles through his first two preseason games, that likely is a vote of confidence from Steichen and the Colts offensive coaching staff that Richardson Sr. is currently in the driver’s seat for the Colts primary backup quarterback job, with the loser between him and Leonard being relegated to the team’s QB3 job. That being said, there’s still one preseason game left to play, so if Richardson Sr. has a bad showing in the first half, and Leonard plays well with the 3s in the second half, perhaps it’s an open-ended competition again—as neither challenger has been able to clearly distance himself from the other so far in training camp and preseason. Still, even though Richardson Sr. hasn’t been great, he’s shown the dynamic ability to make plays with his speed, athleticism, and legs, which is part of what made him so intriguing as a draft prospect when the Colts selected him with the 4th overall pick in the 2023 NFL Draft. He has starting experience under his belt and is entering his 4th year within Steichen’s offense, so he could potentially be considered one of the better backups in the league. The question for the Colts becomes whether they’ll eventually receive a trade offer with meaningful enough value in return to consider moving Richardson Sr., and how much already limited backup practice reps they plan on investing in a quarterback, who more than likely has no intentions of re-signing here once his rookie contract expires at year-end—having already requested a trade from Indianapolis earlier this offseason.

title: Colts wideout Alec Pierce is close to making his return to the practice field
summary: According to head coach Shane Steichen, Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Alec Pierce is expected to return to the practice field this week—if all goes according to plan (via ESPN’s Stephen Holder): Recovering from minor ankle/heel clean-up surgery earlier this offseason, the Colts lucratively re-signed lead wideout has remained on PUP throughout all of training camp […]
full_text: WESTFIELD, IN - AUGUST 20: Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Alec Pierce (14) watches a drill during the Indianapolis Colts and Atlanta Falcons joint training camp practice on August 20, 2026 at the Grand Park Sports Campus in Westfield, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images According to head coach Shane Steichen, Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Alec Pierce is expected to return to the practice field this week—if all goes according to plan (via ESPN’s Stephen Holder): Good news: Colts WR Alec Pierce (ankle) is expected to return to practice this week if all goes to plan, according to coach Shane Steichen. Relatedly, cornerback Charvarius Ward (back) will practice today. — Stephen Holder (@HolderStephen) August 25, 2026 Recovering from minor ankle/heel clean-up surgery earlier this offseason, the Colts lucratively re-signed lead wideout has remained on PUP throughout all of training camp and preseason to-date, unable to participate in organized on-the-field activities. There was initially a four-to-six month timetable of recovery for Pierce’s injury after he underwent minor surgery in late March of this offseason. While Pierce won’t be participating in the Colts preseason home finale this weekend by any means—as he will still have to ramp up his conditioning and see how his ankle/heel physically responds, his return to the practice field makes a still hopeful target date of the Colts regular season home opener against the Baltimore Ravens on Sunday, September 13th potentially in play—which was the team’s expectation all along. His return will be a big boost to a Colts receiving corps that otherwise lacks a bona fide WR1, even with the late training camp veteran addition of Keenan Allen. Pierce provides an elite deep threat, with the ability to separate vertically, high-point the football, and make acrobatic, contested catches—routinely winning ‘50-50’ balls. The Colts don’t have any other wide receiver on their roster like him, and to be fair, not many NFL teams do. He’s expected to be featured much more collectively within their passing offense too this season, having only continued to improve his route tree since entering the league back in 2022. How long it will take for him to fully regain his prior physical form without any training camp, veteran minicamp, and organized team activities earlier in the offseason remains to be seen. Still, it’s a positive injury update for the Colts and Pierce going forward with the regular season rapidly approaching. Other Colts injuries of note are that Colts cornerback Charvarius Ward (back) will practice today along with running back DJ Giddens (hamstring) , while tight end Tyler Warren is nursing a groin injury that may keep him out of practice this week. Fellow tight end Will Mallory (thumb) could be in jeopardy of missing the Colts regular season opener .

title: Colts look in preseason form.
summary: There is not much sugar coating the Atlanta game, but it is not as bad when you are not expecting mid-season form. I saw a couple of things that can’t make their way to regular season, but I saw a lot of searching for answers as well. From most reports, we used mostly second stringers […]
full_text: There is not much sugar coating the Atlanta game, but it is not as bad when you are not expecting mid-season form. I saw a couple of things that can’t make their way to regular season, but I saw a lot of searching for answers as well. From most reports, we used mostly second stringers against Atlanta’s second stringers. Once the regular season starts, all we need is for individual second stringers to fill in well for a starter, not to win our 2nd 22 versus other team’s 2nd 22s. No news here, but with a roster of around 90 that has to be finalized at 53, along with your 16 Practice Squad players, we will cut 20 or so players. One note, PS squads must contain at least 10 1st year players or rookies, but can have up to six players with unlimited experience. Much is made about who is placed on the practice squad and how tenuous their ability to stay there would be. One thing to remember is that a team can’t poach one of your PS players to their own PS. If they select one of your players, they have to be placed on their 53 man roster. So the preseason is mostly about who gets cut. I think that I saw some questions trying to be answered. Did anyone notice that most of the first half saw an interior line of LG Tucker, C Kreutz, and RB Morrissey? I think Tucker was just out there for some LG run to add to his RG and Center work, while Morrissey got time at guard to check his ability beyond backup Center. I think Kreutz found his way to the cut line, but I’m not trying to say who makes the team or not. I am saying that I think they are trying to figure out which nine OL should make the 53, based on providing the best backup at five positions. I also think that Ajiake was being given an audition to begin the season as a starter, with the green dot. He started and played quite a bit with that designation and had pretty good game. Allen also wore the dot when he got his snaps. The fact that Allen played means two things. One, he hasn’t practiced enough as a rookie and secondly, he hasn’t secured the starting position that most expected him to fill immediately. That adds to why I believe Ajiake is being given that opportunity. The defense wasn’t good as a whole, so maybe he didn’t do the green dot job so well? One thing that I am noticing is that our DEs are putting a hand in the dirt less often. It let’s them move a little more, prior to the snap, in an attempt to find the best rushing angle. It also allows them to drop in coverage, which is a tactic that Lou likes, as evidenced by Latu’s three interceptions last year. When trying to sort out what sort of rotation we might see, or even who makes the final 53 man roster, paying attention to who looks best in coverage, might be the tie-breaker. Curry and Gumbs look the part, but that could be because of jersey numbers in the 50s, more than anything tangible that I have witnessed. We will obviously give JT the ball often, but I am now worrying about depth. McGowan may be all we need back there, but the availability of others has me wondering if a bargain vet may be necessary? Another worry is that many see both Blackmon and Edwards making the team. I still think Jones and Carter might be the better way to go, as even second string QBs are playing “Where’s Waldo”, when targeting our defenders. One other slight concern is that we didn’t bring in a camp body to spell Rigo. I know that you can pick up punters off of the street, but I also know that we lost him for a year once, so it might not have been a bad idea to have had a guy in camp that you kept on speed dial. I guess it wouldn’t be a Colts piece, if I didn’t mention the QBs. To start with, if we lose our starter, our chances at competing are greatly diminished. Maybe both would look amazing with the starters, but I do not see either of them looking as good as Jones looked piloting the ship last year. My hope is that any drama associated with the status of our QB2, is limited to depth charts and game day designations. I still wont be shocked if we get a call from a team that loses their QB1 and finally makes an offer for Richardson that Ballard would accept. All in all, I’m just like everyone else who is waiting to see if we get starters for a quarter against the Lions, or at least a couple of drives? I feel better about the depth than you would expect after the kind of beating we took against the Falcons, but as an optimist, that shouldn’t be unexpected. So, the question this week is, “Did our performance against Atlanta change your perception of the Colts as we approach opening day?

title: 10 Observations from Day 1 of Jaguars, Buccaneers Joint Practices
summary: The Tampa Bay Buccaneers arrived at the Miller Electric Center on Tuesday for the first of two joint practice sessions with the Jacksonville Jaguars, and within the first two plays of organized team work, the session had already produced a touchdown, a shoulder scare, and a full-team scuffle. Here is a complete breakdown of our […]
full_text: The Tampa Bay Buccaneers arrived at the Miller Electric Center on Tuesday for the first of two joint practice sessions with the Jacksonville Jaguars, and within the first two plays of organized team work, the session had already produced a touchdown, a shoulder scare, and a full-team scuffle. Here is a complete breakdown of our takeaways from Day 1. 1. BTJ Injury Scare Tuesday carried meaningful personal significance for Brian Thomas Jr. even before a snap was taken. Two years ago, a joint practice against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers served as a clear turning point in what had been a difficult rookie training camp. On Tuesday, he made a similar early entrance. On the very first play of 11-on-11 work, Trevor Lawrence connected with Thomas on an incredible diving touchdown catch at the back of the end zone that brought both sidelines to attention. However, on the play, Thomas landed hard on his shoulder. He came back for one additional play before being pulled to the sideline, where the training staff checked him out for an extended stretch. Liam Coen addressed the situation after practice, saying Thomas came down on his shoulder and that the team will be cautious with him heading into the week, with the goal of getting him fully ready for Cleveland in Week 1. 2. Tempers Flare Early Joint practices have a reputation for physical intensity, and Tuesday had no shortage of moments. Anton Harrison was involved in a scuffle on the second play of practice. Shortly after, Buccaneers tackle DeMonte Capehart exchanged punches with Wyatt Milum. Yet, the biggest moment came when Bhayshul Tuten broke off a 15-yard run and Walker Little stumbled into Buccaneers linebacker Alex Anzalone, which ignited a larger skirmish. Punches were thrown by Tuten and a Tampa Bay defensive back, and Trevor Lawrence stepped in, physically pulling Anzalone away from the pile. The crowd reacted loudly to the hair on hair battle. 3. Josh Cameron Steps Up With Thomas sidelined for the majority of practice and Jakobi Meyers not participating, Cameron and CJ Williams absorbed a significant volume of work Tuesday. Cameron had the bigger individual day of the two, catching a red-zone, scramble drill touchdown from Lawrence, and also hauling in two passes in two-minute drill work, including a 20-yard contested catch through traffic in the middle of the zone. He continues to demonstrate the strong hands that have made him a consistent training camp standout. 4. Parker and Strange Chop Wood With the receiver room shorthanded, Washington and Strange took over on Tuesday. Washington had arguably the play of the day on offense, climbing the ladder in the red zone to outjump cornerback Jacob Parrish and safety Antoine Winfield Jr. for a contested catch that drew a strong reaction from the offensive sideline. He added two more gains of 30-plus yards, one on a crosser and another on a deep out-breaking route. He continues to look every bit of the Jaguars’ number 1 receiver for 2026. Strange was equally sharp, bringing in a difficult back-shoulder throw from Lawrence down the sideline for 40 yards and adding two more catches in traffic for first downs in a later period. The tight end room has been one of the more consistent units throughout the multiple offseason joint practices. 5. Run Game Ramps Up The Bhayshul Tuten story of the day was a two-act performance. In the first act, Antoine Winfield Jr. came up and punched the ball free on contact, a fumble that landed as a reminder of the ball security narrative that followed Tuten throughout his 2025 NFL Draft process. In the second act, he bounced a run to the outside, hit the sideline, and went 50 yards with only one Buccaneers defender able to get a hand on him, and that defender barely grazed his shoulder. Obviously, the ball security will be something to watch as we head into the regular season. Chris Rodriguez added a complementary outside run of his own, finding a hole and bouncing it to the edge for a solid gain, to add to multiple strong red-zone runs. The backfield is still a timeshare built on two very different skill sets, and Tuesday showcased both at their best (and potential worst) simultaneously. 6. Both Pass Rushes Find Success Jacksonville’s recently shuffled offensive line gave Buccaneers defensive tackle Calijah Kancey genuine opportunities, and he converted often in the teams period. Kancey got to Lawrence twice in 11-on-11 with sacks, with the Buccaneers adding a third would-be sack during the two-minute drill. That production line was also reflected in the defensive line, offensive line one-on-one period. The cumulative count for Tampa Bay sacks during teams was three to four would-be takedowns, depending on the source. While the day was an overall success for the Jacksonville offense, this was one area of clear concern. This D-line is going to be a PROBLEM for QBs 💪 pic.twitter.com/DOfRIxR2ob — Tampa Bay Buccaneers (@Buccaneers) August 25, 2026 If there was a player of the day on either roster, the answer was not close. Josh Hines-Allen went 5-for-6 in one-on-one pass rush drills, including a win against All-Pro right tackle Tristan Wirfs that was one of the more impressive individual reps of the entire training camp period. In team periods, he followed that up by recording no fewer than four sacks, including a strip sack in a late period. 41 off the edge, that's a scary sight 🫣 @Dream_Finders | #DUUUVAL pic.twitter.com/hZUK0V9eNV — Jacksonville Jaguars (@Jaguars) August 25, 2026 7. It’s Not Just JHA Hines-Allen’s performance headlined a productive day for the Jacksonville front across the board, but it wasn’t only him to show up. Travon Walker also recorded two sacks. Davon Hamilton had a sack and a pressure that forced a Baker Mayfield throwaway. Ruke Orhorhoro added a sack during the two-minute drill. The collective total for Jacksonville was somewhere between six and seven sacks depending on the count, a number that stands in stark contrast to the 27th-ranked sack unit the Jaguars fielded a year ago. Three forced fumbles and two interceptions rounded out a dominant defensive day that had the entire Jacksonville crowd in attendance jumping from start to finish. 8. Bucs Start Hot; Jax D Takes Over To be fair to Tampa Bay, the early portions of the session belonged to their offense. Bucky Irving opened team periods with a long outside run that gave the Buccaneers the first explosive play of the day. Mayfield followed by connecting with Chris Godwin on a deeper throw for a second consecutive Buccaneers explosive play. After those early moments, however, Jacksonville’s defense settled in and the Tampa Bay offense struggled to generate consistent production. Campanile’s unit won the majority of the session convincingly after the opening early periods. Three occasions where the Jacksonville defense forced a fumble, via contact or punchout Two interceptions (one overturned due to penalty) 6-7 sacks One touchdown was surrendered in the teams periods (a Ted Hurst TD) A dominant day by the Jacksonville defense, no matter who’s scoring the match. 9. AJ and Buster Come Up Big One of the most impressive defensive plays of the day carried an official asterisk. Antonio Johnson returned an interception for what would have been a pick-six in the two-minute drill, only for the play to be wiped out by a pass interference penalty on Travis Hunter away from the ball. On the very next snap, Johnson came up with a pass breakup, stripping the ball on the sideline for the incompletion. Cornerback Montaric Brown had his own would-be pick-six on an overthrown, tipped pass breakup via Eric Murray. He also added a forced incompletion covering Ted Hurst in a separate period, jumping with the receiver with a hand through the pocket to end the drive. 🗣️ Put some respect on Buster Brown! Grab tickets to #TBvsJAX : https://t.co/XnjmMS4q7M @Dream_Finders | #DUUUVAL pic.twitter.com/gHCA2a2rzO — Jacksonville Jaguars (@Jaguars) August 25, 2026 10. Hunter’s Mixed…

title: Jaguars WR Brian Thomas Jr. is ‘alright’ after injury scare
summary: Tuesday’s joint practice with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers started with a bang. On the first 11-vs-11 play of Tuesday’s joint practice with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, Jacksonville Jaguars wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr. immediately reminded Bucs defenders of his game-breaking speed by zooming past Zyon McCollum and leaping over the goal line to haul in […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - AUGUST 18: Head coach Liam Coen talks to Brian Thomas Jr. #7 of the Jacksonville Jaguars practices during training camp at Miller Electric Center on August 18, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images) | Getty Images Tuesday’s joint practice with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers started with a bang. On the first 11-vs-11 play of Tuesday’s joint practice with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, Jacksonville Jaguars wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr. immediately reminded Bucs defenders of his game-breaking speed by zooming past Zyon McCollum and leaping over the goal line to haul in a deep pass for six hypothetical points. As quickly as his teammate’s arms rose to celebrate the score, they fell just as fast. Thomas was visibly shaken up after landing awkwardly on his left shoulder to secure the catch. Jacksonville’s starting X receiver got up on his own and even re-entered the scrimmage a play later, but it would be the last action he saw. “I think he’s alright,” head coach Liam Coen said after practice. “I mean, just came down on his shoulder. I think holding him out was smart. Keep him out, and then get him [ready to] go for Cleveland.” Hopefully, Thomas will return well before the Week 1 matchup against the Browns. The Jaguars’ other two starting wideouts, Parker Washington and Jakobi Meyers, have also missed some recent practice time due to undisclosed injuries. And Travis Hunter continues to focus on playing cornerback — despite Meyers and Thomas being largely unavailable, he spent zero time with the offense on Tuesday. Washington stepped up and carried the passing offense for much of the morning practice. The all-too-obvious breakout candidate had several strong-handed catches in all areas of the field, including one in redzone drills when he floated over two defenders to snag a touchdown. While Washington saw extra targets, the extra snaps went to sixth-round rookies Josh Cameron and CJ Williams. The latter was mostly on the field in three-receiver sets; the former got more opportunities with the first-team offense. Cameron took advantage, finishing a touchdown grab in redzone drills and two contested catches in two-minute drills, but it was more of a “good, he didn’t flop” outing than a “he definitely needs more touches” performance. Both rookies struggled to separate from defenders, and there was one play where Cameron got tangled up with Washington on a deep route concept. “There was a couple things that I think we might’ve jacked up out there,” said Coen. “I know they’re blocking their tails off. I know Josh had a couple good ones. Probably didn’t get a ton of target work, Parker was probably getting a lot of it, Strange got some more. “But I’ve been pleased with their ability to jump in — in terms of, Jakobi’s down, then BT’s out — being able to go in, and us still operate as an offense, and still be able to be efficient at times. Would like to see us separate maybe a little bit better on some of those second-level throws, but they’re coming along.” Jags fans, let us know your thoughts in the comments below!

title: Jacksonville Jaguars unveil their 2026 NFL Rivalries uniforms
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars revealed their latest alternate uniforms on Tuesday, August 25, to much fanfare. This marks the second wave of the Nike/NFL Rivalries campaign, following a hugely successful launch last year for the entirety of the AFC East and NFC West. This time around, the spotlight shifts to the AFC South and NFC North, […]
full_text: The Jacksonville Jaguars revealed their latest alternate uniforms on Tuesday, August 25, to much fanfare. This marks the second wave of the Nike/NFL Rivalries campaign, following a hugely successful launch last year for the entirety of the AFC East and NFC West. This time around, the spotlight shifts to the AFC South and NFC North, and the Jaguars may have just stolen the show when it comes to their division. Prepare yourself for a new look hitting the field at EverBank Stadium in Week 8. When the Jaguars host the Colts on November 1, they’ll premiere the team’s brand-new uniform combo in front of the home crowd as part of the new Nike/NFL Rivalries campaign. A 𝗯𝗼𝗹𝗱 look for our Bold City 😤 #DUUUVAL pic.twitter.com/cgPbnhT6vg — Jacksonville Jaguars (@Jaguars) August 25, 2026 The new uniforms feature a fresh take on Jacksonville’s identity, swapping the usual black and teal for a natural, cream-toned canvas and the first teal helmet in team history. This is also the first uniform to carry a new script “Jaguars” wordmark at the yoke. Pay close attention to the back of the collar, where “Bold City” and “Since ’95” are stitched into the neckline — a quiet nod to the city and the franchise’s roots, worn right at the nape of the neck. On the sleeve, the team opted for a muted take on the modern Jaguars logo, though many fans were hoping for the old-school throwback mark instead. Nike stuck with the current logo, but gave it a toned-down, subdued finish that fits the rest of the uniform. A new vision with a nod to our roots. #DUUUVAL pic.twitter.com/TyhfIWDTrf — Jacksonville Jaguars (@Jaguars) August 25, 2026 The look leans into what the team is calling Bold City Glow: gold accents and iridescent trim finishes designed to capture the neon glow of Jacksonville itself. Nike went Matte Meets Gloss on the numbering, playing matte against gloss to add depth and turn up the volume on DUUUVAL. And the boldest swing of all sits inside the numbers themselves — a black jaguar print pattern trimmed in teal. The pants are also in that black jaguar print design with a teal stripe. It’s Loud & Proud by design, echoing the ferocity teased in the team’s tattoo-shop preview and bringing real cultural flourish to Bold City football. After early rumors pointed toward more of a beach-themed direction, this one lands as a pleasant surprise — a look that actually feels like Jacksonville and Bold City. The jerseys will be available for purchase online very soon: Game jerseys will be $160, and Limited jerseys will be $225 at Fanatics. Like any uniform release, there will be fans who don’t like them, but all in all, I think these will go over well. If the Jaguars’ own teaser is any indication, fortune favors the bold — and Jacksonville just proved it. What are your thoughts on the Jaguars’ Nike Rivalries uniforms? Let us know in the comments

title: Jaguars Reacts Survey: Are you comfortable with Nick Mullens as QB2?
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Jaguars fans and fans across the country. The Jacksonville Jaguars spent over a decade in quarterback purgatory until Trevor Lawrence seized the crown as QB1. Duval County finally feels good about its starting […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - AUGUST 21: Jacksonville Jaguars quarterback Nick Mullens (14) looks for a receiver from the pocket in the first half during the NFL preseason game between the Carolina Panthers and the Jacksonville Jaguars on Friday, August 21, 2206 at EverBank Stadium in JAcksonville, FL (Photo by Peter Joneleit/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Jaguars fans and fans across the country. The Jacksonville Jaguars spent over a decade in quarterback purgatory until Trevor Lawrence seized the crown as QB1. Duval County finally feels good about its starting signal caller… but there is some skepticism about QB2 Nick Mullens. His all-but-guaranteed roster spot is being called into question after a poor performance in the first week of preseason. Mullens completed just 3 of 7 passes for 33 yards and an interception to finish with a brutal 17.9 passer rating. He also took a bad sack on 3rd down despite having multiple receivers open. Two key plays for Jaguars QB Nick Mullens vs the Saints First and 10 – int 3rd and 5 – sack pic.twitter.com/VJA4BPWHDx — Duval Dive- A Jaguars Podcast (@TheDuvalDive) August 16, 2026 So after undrafted rookie quarterback Joey Aguilar flashed in the second week of preseason with a 152.1 passer rating, the question in town is: should the Jaguars consider using a roster spot on Aguilar — or another young, toolsy passer to compete for QB2 duties behind Lawrence? Maybe offer the Colts a seventh-round pick for Anthony Richardson? Personally, I think the Jaguars will have a hard time demoting Mullens. He may not have the athletic traits of someone like Aguilar or Richardson, but what he does have is experience. Mullens was on Liam Coen’s Jaguars last season, Kevin O’Connell’s Vikings for three seasons, and Kyle Shanahan’s 49ers for four seasons. There’s a ton of schematic carryover in those offenses. If Lawrence misses any time this season, the Jaguars would want to play someone who can maximize the playbook. To a lot of people, that means having someone with the physical ability to hypothetically execute any assignment. To the Jaguars, that might mean having someone with the scheme familiarity to dependably execute any assignment. Sign up here to participate in the weekly emailed surveys: Let us know your thoughts in the comments below!

According to Ian Rapoport of NFL Network, the Chiefs are sending a 2028 seventh-round pick to the New York Giants in return for guard Joshua Ezeudu. […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - OCTOBER 20: Joshua Ezeudu #75 of the New York Giants in action against the Philadelphia Eagles during their game at MetLife Stadium on October 20, 2024 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Al Bello/Getty Images) | Getty Images Throughout two preseason contests, it would be an understatement to say that the Kansas City Chiefs ’ backup offensive linemen have underwhelmed. The team apparently shares some concerns with fans . According to Ian Rapoport of NFL Network , the Chiefs are sending a 2028 seventh-round pick to the New York Giants in return for guard Joshua Ezeudu. The #Giants are trading G Joshua Ezeudu to the #Chiefs for a 2028 7th rounder, per me and @MikeGarafolo . Some depth to KC. pic.twitter.com/EerW7sJryt — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) August 26, 2026 The Giants selected Ezeudu in the third round (67th overall) of the 2022 NFL Draft. The 6-foot-4, 310-pound North Carolina product has appeared in 33 games over his first three seasons in New York, with ten starts. He has played at both left guard and left tackle. Ezeudu did not play in 2025 due to a calf injury. He re-signed with the Giants in March. Kansas City will need to make a corresponding move to put Ezeudu on the 90-man roster. The Chiefs currently have 15 offensive linemen on their active roster ahead of Sunday’s mandatory cutdown to 53 players. Editor’s Note: Shoutout to Jared for getting this news out while Arrowhead Pride’s site manager was passed out on the couch by 7:00 p.m. I just wanted to add further context on Ezeudu: he has lined up at left tackle for 402 regular-season snaps, and left guard for 317 regular-season snaps, according to Pro Football Focus. In his most recent active seasons, 2024 and 2023, he was primarily a left tackle. Over four seasons at North Carolina, Ezeudu played left guard for 1,247 snaps, left tackle for 508 snaps and right tackle for 171.
