title: Seahawks roster 2026: Julian Love, Dante Fowler Jr., Beau Stephens are underrated
summary: Some organizations prefer to keep things relatively under the radar. The Seattle Seahawks are not one of those organizations. Soon after the Super Bowl LX win, it was announced that the Seahawks would participate in HBO’s “Hard Knocks” franchise, which could be a recipe for distraction for most people. But general manager John Schneider and […]
full_text: Seattle Seahawks' safety Julian Love holds the Vince Lombardi trophy during the Seattle Seahawks' Superbowl LX victory parade in Seattle, Washington, on February 11, 2026. (Photo by Jason Redmond / AFP via Getty Images) | AFP via Getty Images Some organizations prefer to keep things relatively under the radar. The Seattle Seahawks are not one of those organizations. Soon after the Super Bowl LX win , it was announced that the Seahawks would participate in HBO’s “Hard Knocks” franchise, which could be a recipe for distraction for most people. But general manager John Schneider and head coach Mike Macdonald have built this particular team on the notion that the people on this roster, and in the building overall, are not “most people.” Certainly since the Legion of Boom, the Seahawks have had no issue talking loud and saying everything. Still, there are differences between the LOB and the new M.O.B. — as Richard Sherman learned in a recent conversation with Macdonald that was captured for HBO’s interests. Mike Macdonald kept it real with Richard Sherman about the Seahawks' hunger level 🗣️ @RSherman_25 New Hard Knocks: Training Camp with the @seahawks Tuesday at 9pm ET on @hbomax pic.twitter.com/DumH5hRtpe — NFL (@NFL) August 17, 2026 When I interviewed Macdonald for the Athlon Sports NFL preview magazine this offseason , he went a bit deeper into the mentality that allows the Seahawks to maintain that ultimate competitive edge without getting too… well, edgy in the wrong direction. Especially now that the Seahawks have the opportunity to become the ninth franchise and the 10th team in NFL history to repeat as Super Bowl champs. “I have reached out to some people who have won back-to-back championships,” he told me. “And it’s been great advice, but I think the thing that we learned last year is like, look, we want to do it our way with how we go about our business every day, and what’s best for the Seahawks. It’s great to learn from other people, but by no means are we trying to copy other people’s style or trying to do it that way. The overarching thing is, it’s the same destination, but the journey is completely different with a completely different set of people. “Even for the people that were here last year … I mean, it’s different viewpoints, and it’s different experiences that are under their belts. We’re going to have a lot of new people joining us from other teams who lost some great players. So to me, we’re saying that instead of running it back or defending anything, we want to run our process forward. How do we be us and take the next version of us as a team forward, and do that every day? I don’t think that our process or our viewpoint about who we want to become, or how we get there, changes because of the Super Bowl or what we evolved to in terms of what we did every day and what our mentality was because it was the end of the season. I think you keep that same mentality of what we’re trying to achieve every day. Even though now it’s the 2026 season, it’s all the same thought process about how we want to be us as Seahawks. And there are going to be different challenges that we’re going to face along the road. We know that going in, but in no way are we saying that we’re defending anything. “Let’s just try to nail being us as well as we can, and stack those days. And then once we get to the season, we’ll go from there.” So, the hay is just about in the barn for a team that returns 21 of its 22 starters from last season’s championship team, with Kenneth Walker as the obvious defector and first-round pick Jadarian Price as his ostensibly able replacement. Still, Super Bowl teams require a perfect storm of guys you expect to be great, and guys who pop up out of nowhere to be great when it’s needed the most. To that end, I’ve identified three Hidden Gems for the 2026 Seahawks — one underrated veteran, one underrated free-agent signing, and one underrated draft pick. Now… time to run it forward. Loudly. Underrated veteran: Safety Julian Love There’s always a lot of talk about the Seahawks’ secondary, but most of it (at least on a national scale) tends to overlook the guy who was the most effective in that secondary when healthy last season. Last season in 11 games (he missed multiple games with a hamstring injury), Love allowed nine catches on 21 targets for 83 yards, 39 yards after the catch, no touchdowns, two interceptions, five pass breakups, and an opponent passer rating of 17.7 — by far the lowest of any safety who played at least 50% of his team’s snaps in 2025 — Cole Bishop of the Buffalo Bills finished second at 45.7. Love can play all over the field, and he proved that when Nick Emmanwori was dealing with an ankle injury in the days before the Super Bowl. Love told anybody who would listen that if Emmanwori couldn’t go, he’d play nickel, or wherever he was most needed. Turned out that Emmanwori did go, and that allowed Love to not only play his usual (primarily deep-third) roles, but also to nab a game-sealing interception, and explain after the game why the Seahawks were able to play dime defense with six defensive backs on the field on 40 of their 72 defensive snaps — an insane rate for any NFL game, much less the most important game of the year. Postgame, I asked Seahawks safety Julian Love to explain to me how it is that Mike Macdonald is able to call defenses that other teams only wish they could. pic.twitter.com/7xA04xd5sf — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) February 9, 2026 “That’s Julian, he’s the Mayor, man,” Macdonald said in June when asked about Love saying he’ll play wherever is best for the defense. “One of our leaders on our team, and that exemplifies the mentality we’re looking for out of all of our guys. It’s never really a question with Julian, you just assume he’s going to feel that way, and that’s a testament to who he is every day. We’re never trying to take away from his ability to make plays or get him away from the action. We’re always thinking about, ‘How do we get him closer to the action?’ Sometimes, because he is so talented and so versatile, you do have to put him in other situations to round out the 11 and make sure we’re the best 11 out there, but the fact that that’s not an issue just makes us a better team, so that’s just a testament to him.” As the NFL has turned to the two-high revolution, with subtle and not-so-subtle coverage switches out of that, Love has become the best option on the team who does it better than anybody else. The 2019 fourth-round pick of the New York Giants, who signed a two-year, $12 million contract with the Seahawks in 2023, and then a three-year, $33 million extension in 2024, is the very model of the modern deep-third defender. Was Julian Love of the @Seahawks the NFL's best coverage safety in 2025? The answer lies somewhere between "yes" and "yes." pic.twitter.com/zZclsvXCJ8 — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 23, 2026 Leonard Williams, whose time with Love goes back to the Giants from 2019-2022, is well-versed in his friend’s leadership, and what it means. “To me he’s always been that guy, which is so special,” Williams recently said. “I got to the Giants his rookie year, and he’s been the same guy. He’s one of those guys that… he has a process. He’s going to show up to work with enthusiasm every day. To me over time, the biggest growth I’ve seen is everyone else noticing it. That’s what is so cool; he’s finally getting his flowers — he has been for a few years now, I know that, but it’s cool for me to see someone that I’ve seen at a young age grow into a respected player in the league. We were just sharing about that the other day at practice, that we’ve played with each other for eight years now. That’s the longest I’ve ever played with anybody.” Everybody who knows about Julian Love on and off the field respects him. It’s time that more people knew about the best coverage safety in the business. Underrated free agent: EDGE Dante Fowler Jr. So, the Seahawks are set…
author: Doug Farrar

title: Seahawks Reacts Survey: Will Jalen Milroe make the 53-man roster?
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Seahawks fans and fans across the country. The Seattle Seahawks have some significant question marks regarding their team depth after losing Bud Clark, Jake Bobo, and Mason Richman to serious injuries. Naturally, this […]
full_text: Aug 23, 2026; Nashville, Tennessee, USA; Seattle Seahawks quarterback Jalen Milroe (6) throws a pass against the Tennessee Titans during the second half at Nissan Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Steve Roberts-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Seahawks fans and fans across the country. The Seattle Seahawks have some significant question marks regarding their team depth after losing Bud Clark, Jake Bobo, and Mason Richman to serious injuries. Naturally, this week’s Seahawks Reacts is about Jalen Milroe, because that’s who has garnered most of the preseason attention. Milroe has not been very good in his second preseason. The sacks have been bad, the two interceptions against the Tennessee Titans were brutal, and he’s not really looked like someone with the ceiling of being an NFL starting quarterback. And yet, he’s still a third-round pick and on a cheap rookie contract, so the Seahawks might be willing to give it another year of development before making a grander decision on his future. There’s no need to be impatient like he’s a top-five pick. The interesting aspect of Milroe’s roster status for 2026 is whether or not he’s expendable due to a combination of his development (or, maybe not developing as well as hoped) and the Seahawks having needs elsewhere on the team. Does it make sense to keep a third quarterback, cheap and physically talented as he may be, if it comes at the cost of an extra cornerback or safety or receiver? If Milroe looked like QB2 over Drew Lock at the very least, this isn’t a debate. It’s probably a debate we’ll continue to have until something changes. The question is “Will Jalen Milroe make the Seahawks’ 53-man roster?” Divorce yourself from what you want to happen and predict what you think will happen. Is he going to be QB3 again? Will he be waived—in a quarterback-needy world, I think he does get claimed—or will he be traded? Vote in the survey below! That would mean Jones returns this upcoming weekend and can participate in the three sessions before the 49ers fly to Australia on Wednesday, September 2. Kurtis Rourke won’t play this Thursday as he recovers from a rib injury. Shanahan said Rourke’s injury wasn’t as bad as the one Jordan James suffered. Rourke had three broken ribs. He’ll still miss the preseason finale, but will return to practice next weekend, according to Shanahan.” Kawakami: What happens to the 49ers if Jed York turns into an absentee owner? (Paywall) “And indications that York recently moved away from the Bay Area back to the Youngstown, Ohio, area where he grew up could have the biggest ramifications of all. But for the here and now — and for Melbourne, Australia, against the Rams on Sept. 10 — the York headlines, questions, and think pieces are, in Kyle Shanahan’s words on Tuesday, “kind of irrelevant to our guys.” That was definitely a bit of a swat-away for an uncomfortable topic by a coach who has many other things on his plate; but Shanahan was also not incorrect. York set this up a long time ago — Shanahan and John Lynch run every aspect of the football side, obviously with some financial and philosophical oversight from York, but not that much….And part of the reason Lynch and Shanahan know they can operate freely and without worrying about getting overruled or second-guessed is that they have such a direct relationship with York. If York recedes into the Ohio shadows, that is, on one hand, the dream scenario for a coach and GM, who could essentially be acting as dual owners. But also, if York isn’t there to hear all of their deliberations, if he doesn’t chime in a time or two to help get to a conclusion, he might feel a little disassociated from Shanahan and Lynch. The deep ties could get tested. It’s also a step closer to the York family as a whole feeling more distant from everybody else — which could lead to possibly considering a huge offer to sell the team; until now, I believe it’s been Jed York’s passion and financial success that’s eliminated any cash-out consideration.”

title: As new details emerge in Jed York’s case, Kyle Shanahan speaks to the media
summary: As the San Francisco 49ers deal with the fallout from owner Jed York’s arrest in Ohio in connection with a prostitution sting, new details have been revealed by 49ers insider Matt Barrows. York pleaded no contest Monday morning to two misdemeanor charges and spent two days in jail. Barrows reported in his latest for the […]
full_text: As the San Francisco 49ers deal with the fallout from owner Jed York’s arrest in Ohio in connection with a prostitution sting, new details have been revealed by 49ers insider Matt Barrows. York pleaded no contest Monday morning to two misdemeanor charges and spent two days in jail. Barrows reported in his latest for the Athletic that York responded to an ad on a prostitution website under the name “Joe.” An agent for the task force in the area placed the ad, and York had spent a day attempting to arrange a meeting. “Driving an Avis rental car, York was seen arriving in the mobile home park,” Barrows wrote. “When he couldn’t find the lot number, he went back onto the main road, where he was stopped by police. According to the report, a test text message showed that York’s phone had been used to set up the meeting. Police seized the phone and the $160. As the 49ers await a decision from the NFL regarding York and a possible fine and/or suspension, head coach Kyle Shanahan took the podium following today’s practice and was asked several questions about York and his legal situation. “I got to talk to Jed the last two days and today,” Shanahan said. “Obviously, it’s a very tough situation. I mean, views for the organization going forward is the same as usual. There won’t be any difference in that. But I know it’s extremely fresh. “I think it’s a very, very personal situation. I’ve got a lot of respect for Jed. I’ve got a lot of respect for Danielle (Jed’s wife). Their family does mean a lot to me. So, with it being this personal, I’m trying as hard as I can to keep it that way.” Shanahan reiterated that there wasn’t a need to deliver a message to the team regarding the situation. The team is business as usual as they will travel to Las Vegas for the preseason finale on Thursday night.
author: Jason Aponte

title: 49ers injury updates: Week 1 takes precedence over the preseason
summary: Today is the second-to-last day for the San Francisco 49ers to evaluate their roster. The battle for left guard remains up in the air. 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan said the team isn’t expecting left guard Robert Jones to return until “around Australia.” The team is hopeful Jones can return to practice before they leave […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - JULY 27: Mike Evans #5 of the San Francisco 49ers works out during training camp practice at SAP Performance Facility on July 27, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Today is the second-to-last day for the San Francisco 49ers to evaluate their roster. The battle for left guard remains up in the air. 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan said the team isn’t expecting left guard Robert Jones to return until “around Australia.” The team is hopeful Jones can return to practice before they leave the States. That would mean Jones returns this upcoming weekend and can participate in the three sessions before the 49ers fly to Australia on Wednesday, September 2. Kurtis Rourke won’t play this Thursday as he recovers from a rib injury. Shanahan said Rourke’s injury wasn’t as bad as the one Jordan James suffered. Rourke had three broken ribs. He’ll still miss the preseason finale, but will return to practice next weekend, according to Shanahan. Romello Height has missed practice with an ankle injury. Shanahan didn’t expound on that. It’s “possible” Christian Kirk ( calf strain ) could begin the season on the Injured Reserve. Vederian Lowe ( high-ankle sprain ) is another candidate. Both players have been out for about a month now, as their injuries occurred at the end of July. They each signed as free agents this past offseason for what was effectively the veteran minimum. The 49ers were counting on each to be key depth pieces. The team boards a plane three days after their roster shrinks to 53. Kirk and Lowe have as much of a chance to play in Week 1 as Brandon Aiyuk. We’re unlikely to see them for the first month of the season. The Injured Reserve list is something the 49ers will lean into. They have eight designations to return during the regular season. You also don’t waste a roster spot on these players. They can afford to be patient with Kirk and Lowe, even if it’s for the first four games of the season — the minimum games a player must sit out if he begins the season on the Injured Reserve. Shanahan spoke about weighing the health of his roster ahead of roster cuts: “Most of our guys, besides Ricky and everything, are going to be all right. How good are they Week 1? How good are they going to be Week 2? Those are things that we’ve got to battle out. “But when you know they’re going to be healthy within those first four weeks, then it’s not as complicated. It’s frustrating, because you’d like ‘em to be there right away. But if they’re not going to be healthy after four weeks, then you can decide about PUP and things like that.” Speaking of the PUP, Mykel Williams might be a PUP candidate. This year’s rule change allows any player on the reserve/PUP list to begin their 21-day practice period after the team’s second regular-season game. Shanahan stressed the importance of having two veterans you can designate to return from Injured Reserve when it comes down to roster cuts. It’s worth noting that will automatically count toward the eight designated returns, but using that for two veterans makes the most sense The plan is to get Nick Bosa into practice next weekend. Shanahan said Bosa is doing well. George Kittle has been participating in the non-competitive periods of practice. He’s running routes on air, but it doesn’t sound like Kittle is involved in any of the heavy-contact portions of practice. That will change during the next block of practices after the 49ers’ mandatory three days off. Mike Evans did not practice today with a tight groin. Jacob Cowing also did not practice because of a groin injury. Shanahan is hoping to get Evans back at practice next week; he said, “Same with Mike,” when asked when Cowing would return. Week 1 is right around the corner for the 49ers. There’s little reason to risk your star players getting dinged up in practice with a division game in two weeks. That quick turnaround is why we’re not going to see many of the starters on Thursday: “I don’t think you’ll see many starters. We just don’t have enough time as we usually do, so I’ll be surprised if any of them are out there. There might be a couple. But it’ll be closer to how Week 1 looked.” Right guard Dominick Puni complained about having residual effects of a concussion after practice. Shanahan said Puni’s “most likely back in” the concussion protocol. Upton Stout didn’t practice because of a hip flexor. He’s also expected to return next week. According to The Athletic’s Matt Barrows, 24 players didn’t practice in full on Tuesday. The 49ers are a week and a day away from getting on a plane for the longest trip they’ll take all season. Shanahan said the biggest challenges of this trip are having enough time and staying healthy. The 49ers are doing everything they can to control the injury variable ahead of Week 1.
author: Kyle Posey

title: Can the 49ers afford to keep 3 quarterbacks with their injuries?

The San Francisco 49ers will have some difficult decisions to make next Sunday as they attempt to trim their roster to 53. As always, injuries will play a major factor. How many games will Mykel Williams miss? Will there be a new injury by Sunday? Does the team need to keep extra bodies at a position for one reason or another? Because of that, the 49ers are likely to skimp at certain positions. Tight end and safety are the obvious ones. But what about quarterback? Kurtis Rourke looked the part in the first preseason game. No position is more valuable than quarterback. Rourke was a seventh-rounder, but that’s because he was going to miss his rookie year. The 49ers would be fortunate if Rourke made it through waivers. He’s likely Brock Purdy’s backup after the 2026 season. But in the same breath, there would need to be a 2022-type of injury-riddled season for Rourke to play. The Niners’ brass must decide if Rourke’s future is worth a roster spot on a team with depth questions. It’ll help if multiple players can do multiple jobs. Linebackers, tight ends, running backs, and receivers at the bottom of the depth chart covering kicks will go a long way. title: One training camp battle between stars has 49ers fired up
summary: When it comes to training camp every year, there’s usually one San Francisco 49ers star in the middle of the action: linebacker Fred Warner. Known for his hard-hitting style and smack talk, Warner has frequently engaged in verbal and physical battles in training camp, testing his teammates while making plays as one of the 49ers […]
full_text: TAMPA, FL - OCTOBER 12: Fred Warner #54 of the San Francisco 49ers fires up the team on the field before the game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Raymond James Stadium on October 12, 2025 in Tampa, Florida. The Buccaneers defeated the 49ers 30-19. (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images When it comes to training camp every year, there’s usually one San Francisco 49ers star in the middle of the action: linebacker Fred Warner. Known for his hard-hitting style and smack talk, Warner has frequently engaged in verbal and physical battles in training camp, testing his teammates while making plays as one of the 49ers top defenders. On the other side of that battle? Brock Purdy, who has gone up against Warner every training camp of his career, making for some strong battles between the offense and the defense. Well, things got feisty over the weekend, as Purdy and Warner had a back-and-forth in camp that really was on display on Sunday. According to ESPN’s Nick Wagoner, the two sides were frequently making plays and letting the other hear it. Purdy had a nice layered throw to Mike Evans over Warner, who later responded by breaking up a pass to Demarcus Robinson, while sharing a few words for his quarterback. Purdy fired back with a throw over the middle to Deebo Samuel, once again beating Warner, and the quarterback had some choice words for the star linebacker, firing back. That has been a fun battle all training camp long, and it’s got the team fired up. “I think it’s cool. It’s competitive,” offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak said of Purdy engaging in some of the verbal chatter with Warner. “It’s respect with his teammates that they can do that and shake hands after, and they can line up and compete and try to get the best out of each other. Talk a little smack. But at the end of the day, a lot of respect between those two guys. And that’s why they’re really good players. They go out there, compete every day, and they have an edge, but they’re great teammates at the end of the day.” With injuries looming over the team, having that energy from two leaders on the team can amp up the competitiveness at a crucial point in training camp. “It was a friendly conversation. It’s camp. That’s what it is,” right tackle Colton McKivitz said. “You got 2 competitors. I mean, we’re all competitive, but you’ve got 2 leaders of the team, 2 competitors of the team in a period of practice where we’re in the dog days of camp. I mean, we got 2 [practices] left till the game, and then that’s it. “So it’s kind of one of those practices where, you know, everyone’s a little sore, banged up, tired, but it just means more to some guys. And for them to be jawing back and forth, it’s great for us. It shows everyone’s into it. Everyone cares. There’s a lot of pride in what the drill is. And we’re competing against each other right now. So, the fact that there’s always going to be a little banter and offense versus defense, but we’re just making each other better.” We don’t often hear about that verbal side from Purdy, so it’s a fun sign to see him engage with Warner and win some of those battles on the field.

title: What does the Deion Jones-Zamir White trade mean for the 49ers?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers and New Orleans Saints completed a trade late Sunday night: running back Zamir White to New Orleans in exchange for linebacker Deion Jones. Player-for-player trades aren’t exactly common in the NFL, but what does this trade mean for the 49ers and the linebacker room before the preseason finale against the Las […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 9: Deion Jones #45 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers smiles while wearing “Salute to Service” gear prior to an NFL football game against the New England Patriots at Raymond James Stadium on November 9, 2025 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers and New Orleans Saints completed a trade late Sunday night : running back Zamir White to New Orleans in exchange for linebacker Deion Jones. Player-for-player trades aren’t exactly common in the NFL, but what does this trade mean for the 49ers and the linebacker room before the preseason finale against the Las Vegas Raiders on Thursday night? Firstly, both players were unlikely to make either roster. The Saints are dealing with multiple injuries in their running back room. Alvin Kamara is likely to miss the season opener, and backup running back Devin Neal suffered a hamstring injury during the preseason matchup with the Los Angeles Rams on Saturday. On top of that, Audric Estime has been dealing with foot discomfort throughout the offseason. Simply put, the Saints need healthy bodies to help the team get to the finish line of cutdown day. Acquiring Zamir White makes perfect sense. So, what about Deion Jones? Well, the 49ers are also dealing with injuries in their linebacker room. Nick Martin suffered a hamstring injury, and Special Teams ace Luke Gifford is dealing with his own hamstring strain. It makes sense to bring Jones in given his time under Raheem Morris in 2020, and he can bridge the gap to cutdown day for the 49ers. While it is likely Jones won’t make the 53-man roster, a practice squad stint is also possible. Let’s say the injuries to the linebacker room are more severe and will cost them regular-season time; Jones can be depth at the end of the roster for Morris and the 49ers. During his time with the Falcons in 2020, Jones had his best season as a player, but it was interesting to note how Morris deployed Jones as a pass rusher. On 85 pass-rushing snaps, Jones recorded 19 pressures, five sacks, six QB hits, eight hurries, and a 75.0 pass-rushing grade, according to PFF, which are career highs. This player-for-player deal should be interpreted as band aids for both teams, but Jones could stick on the roster and be help for the younger linebackers learning Morris’s system if the injuries to the other linebackers linger.
author: Jason Aponte

title: 49ers roster 2026: Renardo Green, Dre Greenlaw, Gracen Halton are underrated
summary: As a guest columnist and longtime Niners Nation friend (though I reside in Seattle), I’ll assume that y’all are pretty freaking tired of hearing about the substation. And I’d rather avoid low-hanging fruit. So, let’s move beyond the year-to-year injury thing, and talk about how the 2026 San Francisco 49ers can be at their competitive […]
full_text: As a guest columnist and longtime Niners Nation friend (though I reside in Seattle), I’ll assume that y’all are pretty freaking tired of hearing about the substation. And I’d rather avoid low-hanging fruit. So, let’s move beyond the year-to-year injury thing, and talk about how the 2026 San Francisco 49ers can be at their competitive best, assuming even league-average injury luck… which would be a big upward boost. We do have to mention the preseason injuries, because they matter. George Kittle and Christian McCaffrey appear to be ready for work again , which is nice, but losing Ricky Pearsall for the season to a torn PCL in his right knee isn’t great, and there are all kinds of minor nicks and cuts to deal with. Maybe this is the year that the 49ers’ injury luck regresses to the mean — Lord knows, the franchise deserves a break there. Is there enough in the tank to deal with the uber-loaded Seahawks and Rams? There’s always a chance with Kyle Shanahan, who took a limping roster into the playoffs when most coaches would have fallen short (the 41-6 Divisional Round loss to the Seahawks was a fait accompli in that regard), but even getting past the Philadelphia Eagles in the Wild Card round was an accomplishment. But this is also a team that has the NFL’s second-oldest roster coming into the 2026 season , ahead of only the Washington Commanders. Trent Williams is 38 years old. Kyle Juszczyk is 35. Newly-acquired Mike Evans is 33, as is Kittle. McCaffrey is 30, as is Fred Warner, and the returning Deebo Samuel. Nick Bosa and the returning Dre Greenlaw (more on him in a minute) are 29. So, if there’s a window for these 49ers, it may have to be now. Because the reload-to-rebuild story is coming sooner or later. If that window is to be cracked open in 2026, it will require maximum greatness (and availability) from everyone on the roster. Not just all the aforementioned stars, but also the guys whose on-field exploits have exceeded their name recognition in a national sense. To that end, I have three Hidden Gems for the 2026 San Francisco 49ers — one underrated veteran, one underrated free agent, and one underrated draft pick. Underrated veteran: CB Renardo Green I have always had a thing for great aggressive press cornerbacks; perhaps I was indoctrinated by watching Lester Hayes in my youth. So, when I caught Florida State’s Renardo Green’s game tape leading up to the 2024 draft, I was all the way in. Because the Seminoles of the time, under defensive coordinator Adam Fuller, played more press than most college teams, and they did so without a second thought. Green’s ability to lock receivers down in press was a big part of that. Renardo Green, CB, Florida State PLUSES — Green is a complete pain in the ass when he's pressed up on the receiver and follows to the boundary on anything vertical; he'll glue himself to his guy, and he's very tough to shake. Ask Malik Nabers about that re: the video below.… pic.twitter.com/c00VFJvDXi — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) April 7, 2024 Now, when heavy press cornerbacks come into the NFL, it’s not always an easy transition. Pressing and then matching routes with the best receivers on the planet is a boom-and-bust proposition by nature, and you’re not always going to win. In 33 press coverage targets last season per Pro Football Focus, Green allowed 21 catches for 9.6 yards per reception and 2.4 yards of separation per target, with five pass breakups and four explosive plays. Which is why things weren’t always right between Green and Shanahan . Kyle Shanahan chewing out Renardo Green on the sideline 👀 pic.twitter.com/m09Qy6NQvm — Alex Tran (@nineralex) January 18, 2026 To be fair, Green had some evil matchups to deal with. And there were times when he looked like the No. 1 cornerback everyone would like him to be. Pressing Jaxson Smith-Njigba can be an absolute horror movie for any cornerback. Renardo Green of the @49ers took some expected lumps from the NFL's best receiver, but he gave as good as he got. pic.twitter.com/4LlJvYwEwk — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 23, 2026 Now, Green is pretty happy with Raheem Morris as the new defensive coordinator, and the feeling is mutual. “It’s easier to play faster. I feel like he’s finer, more detailed with realistic things,” Green said in June of the transition from Robert Saleh to Morris. “It’s a lot less thinking, and it’s geared towards me and the guys’ strong suits, and what we do well.” Morris, the eternal optimist, sees only good in Green’s potential. Raheem Morris on Renardo Green: “He’s shown the ability to go out there and play at an elite level from off coverage, from bump. He’s shown the ability to take it from the classroom to the field. He made a big time play today. He’s shown up in a big way. He showed up during… pic.twitter.com/V0P3UIlIyB — Coach Yac 🗣 (@Coach_Yac) July 27, 2026 If Green can maximize his tools in Morris’ defense, clamp down on those receivers with a bit more consistency, and carve out those weird moments, it would be a big deal for this defense. As Morris intimated, Green has all the ability to make it happen. Underrated free agent: LB Dre Greenlaw When the 49ers were rolling under Jim Harbaugh and defensive coordinator Vic Fangio back in the early 2010s, their teams were accentuated greatly by the fact that Patrick Willis and NaVorro Bowman, they had the NFL’s best linebacker duo. Under Kyle Shanahan and multiple defensive coordinators from 2019-2024, the 49ers recaptured that magic with the dynamic duo of Fred Warner and Dre Greenlaw. Until they didn’t. Greenlaw’s freak torn Achilles in Super Bowl LVIII led to a 2024 season in which he played a grand total of 34 defensive snaps before the team shut him down. Then, the 2019 fifth-round pick out of Arkansas signed a three-year, $31.5 million contract with the Denver Broncos — a three-year deal that ended after one year when Denver released Greenlaw on March 9. Injuries were an issue to a point — a lingering quadricep injury kept him out until Week 7 — but when he was healthy, he was the Dre Greenlaw one would expect. In 2025, with 386 defensive snaps, he had 27 solo tackles, 13 stops, two tackles for loss, one sack, and three quarterback pressures in 33 pass-rushing reps. In coverage, he gave up 14 catches on 20 targets for 118 yards, 64 yards after the catch, one touchdown, one interception, one pass breakup, and an opponent passer rating of 80.8. Basically, he was him again. Dre Greenlaw when he was healthy last season. I'm guessing Fred Warner is happy that the @49ers got the band back together… pic.twitter.com/oHfid6e7SO — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 23, 2026 Is Fred Warner happy? You could say so. “It’s just been special from the moment he gave me that phone call telling me he was coming back,” Warner recently said . “It’s been super special. Then today, kind of met every expectation. Even days leading up to today, I’ve been having to tell him like, ‘Hey bro, relax,’ because he’s been amped up and ready to go. It’s just great having him back. “Like I’ve always talked about, he’s one of the best football players I’ve ever played with, and his passion for the game, his mentality, having a guy like that beside you just gives you so much confidence as a player to go out there and rock out. It’s great having him back.” Greenlaw is just happy to be back in the fold. “Even when I was gone, I knew that San Fran was still going to have the capability of getting to the playoffs, getting to the Super Bowl, whatever is in store for them,” he said in June . “That’s just because of the guys that’s on the team. You got the best leadership, just great quality of guys here. “I think everything that’s in store that we wanted five years before, we still got that same opportunity now. If anything, I see more of an opportunity for us to do it just because we’re veterans. We’re the vets. We’ve seen everything. It’s just our turn to get it done.” Yes, the 49ers are tempting fate by bringing…

full_text: The Commanders roster turnover continues at a rapid clip, with an important addition to the offensive line. According to a Tuesday evening report from NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport, Washington is signing former Pro Bowl tackle D.J. Humphries. Source: The #Commanders are signing former Pro Bowl LT DJ Humphries to a 1-year deal, adding key depth and starting experience to their O-line. With Laremy Tunsil out with a torn triceps, Humphries — who has 101 career starts mostly with the #AZCardinals — helps. pic.twitter.com/B54N9tS3Rs — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) August 25, 2026 This move should tie in with the release of offensive tackle Foster Sarell , which the Commanders announced earlier Tuesday. Humphries brings tons of experience to a Commanders position group dealing with some significant injuries. Laremy Tunsil’s torn triceps was a major blow that cannot be understated. The early August injury required surgery and will take months to heal and rehabilitate, moving third-year pro Brandon Coleman from a position battle at left guard to left tackle. That thinned Washington’s depth at the position, which Humphries was signed to fortify. He has the experience and savvy to do so, with 101 starts in 108 NFL games . He played eight seasons with the Arizona Cardinals, who made him the No. 24 overall NFL draft pick in 2015. While he has primarily worked at left tackle, he has experience on the right. He earned a Pro Bowl honor following the 2021 campaign. Humphries suffered a torn ACL late in the 2023 season, and was later released by Arizona with a failed physical designation. He signed with the Kansas City Chiefs late in the 2024 season, after being cleared. He also worked for the L.A. Rams in 2025. Humphries offers an upgrade at swing tackle, even if he doesn’t locate pre-injury form. He’ll have a few days to merge into the Commanders system, but it would be a shock if a signing like this doesn’t make the initial 53-man roster and have time to acclimate and find a role in the offensive front.

title: Commanders film session: Three rookies on the rise following Lions game
summary: The Commanders’ overall offensive performance during Saturday’s preseason game in Detroit was uninspiring. That unit finished the game against the Lions scoring just six points. While Washington didn’t get into the end zone in a 17-13 loss, the rookie film told a different story. Quarterback Athan Kaliakmanis showed he can attack the field, running back […]
full_text: The Commanders’ overall offensive performance during Saturday’s preseason game in Detroit was uninspiring. That unit finished the game against the Lions scoring just six points. While Washington didn’t get into the end zone in a 17-13 loss , the rookie film told a different story. Quarterback Athan Kaliakmanis showed he can attack the field, running back Kaytron Allen demonstrated impressive football intelligence and receiver Antonio Williams showed he can win in tight spaces. If you’re general manager Adam Peters, you’re probably smiling after watching some members of the 2026 draft class flash in their snaps against the Detroit Lions. Kaliakmanis may not be Washington’s starting quarterback anytime soon, but he’s stacking one encouraging performance on top of another. Kaliakmanis is stretching the field vertically, making throws on all three levels on the boundary and field sides. It’s a testament to his arm velocity and the confidence he has to attack defenses. Against Detroit, Kaliakmanis faced a lot of man coverage and it led to an explosive day, with 162 passing yards on 11 completions. Allen didn’t have a great day statistically, but his post-snap processing and high-level football instincts complement his vision and elusiveness. It helps overcome his lack of threatening foot speed. Against the Lions, he saved several would-be negative runs, but he also had several runs for positive gains that he created on his own. The key difference between Allen and undrafted rookie Robert Henry Jr. , whom he is currently splitting time with, is his ability to manipulate defenders at the first and second levels to create creases he can exploit. It was also a productive day for Williams, Washington’s third-round pick, who finished his game against the Lions with three catches for 41 yards. To earn playing time and targets during the regular season, Williams needs to prove to quarterback Jayden Daniels that he can be trusted. It comes over time, but Williams continues to earn his stripes the right way. Let’s take a look at a few plays from the Commanders preseason matchup against the Detroit Lions: Allen demonstrates a strong understanding of gap manipulation, as he faces an eight-man box on this play. The Lions defender fills the backside B-gap against Washington’s zone run. Additionally, the Lions are winning at the point of contact with their backside 1-technique defender, who is essentially squeezing the playside gap that Allen is intending to run through. Allen’s hesitation, faking the bend to the backside B-gap before pressing playside, forces the Lions’ 1-tech defender to react and leave his gap slightly enough for Allen to exploit. Some of the better-quality running backs in the NFL display Allen’s traits, making their intentions more difficult for defenders to predict at the line of scrimmage and forcing them to stay as disciplined as possible. In this one play, you see how Allen can make a defense pay if they cannot stay gap-disciplined. Kaliakmanis shows excellent ball placement on one of his best throws of the preseason, a slot fade to rookie Jaden Bradley. Facing man coverage, the middle of the field is closed and Bradley is able to get a step on the slot corner and stem away from the Lions’ single-high safety. Kaliakmanis is able to process the Lions’ coverage pre- and post-snap and capitalize with an explosive play. (And shoutout to Bradley, who made one of the best catches of the preseason.) Kaliakmanis, similar to the completion to Bradley, faces another Cover 1 rep. The rookie quarterback stretches the field again, this time toward the boundary with a 55-yard completion to receiver Nick Nash. Kaliakmanis has good ball placement toward the sideline but also displays impressive velocity to keep the ball in front of Nash, allowing him to run under it. Kaliakmanis’ accuracy wasn’t the best on this play, but this is why wide receivers get paid, too. Williams has a great catch in traffic against tight man coverage. Williams initially creates a subtle separation on his crosser with a stair-step technique, which is used against defenders trailing in man coverage. At the catch point, Williams high-points and adjusts to a pass behind him. It’s a great display of body control and ball security in this situation, but also a great rep to put on tape for Williams, who, while he has a smaller frame, is very much capable of coming up big for his quarterback in contested situations. Kaliakmanis is intriguing, but it isn’t simply off of his arm strength. The combination of his arm talent and willingness to use it raises his stock. Washington has consistently given him opportunities to attack vertically, and he has responded, often showing he can make throws outside the numbers and down the field. He’s proving that his offensive coordinator, David Blough, wouldn’t be limited in their play calling with him under center. Granted, he has not faced many complex coverages; he needs to be exposed to zone coverages and blitzes that will force him to address protection calls pre-snap and make the right read post-snap when fire zones and zone blitzes require him to release the ball quickly. Time will tell as he continues to get more reps, and there will be plenty available during Friday’s preseason game against the Baltimore Ravens. It’s clear that Kaliakmanis has an edge over Sam Hartman and could very well be in line to be Jayden Daniels’ backup whenever Marcus Mariota’s time ends in Washington. Both Allen and Williams have shown their value to the offense as role players; it is encouraging to see flashes early on. For Allen, the question still remains about his foot speed: with more exposure on the field during the regular season and most defenders being starters or second-string, can he continue creating his own lanes and gaining positive yards for the offense if the offensive line doesn’t win? For Williams, his ability to handle physicality remains to be seen. If he is able to play through contact at an acceptable level when the snaps are real, that will certainly increase his effectiveness in this offense, as he’d not need to be continuously schemed open. Again, the Commanders’ offense may have scored just six points, but these three offensive rookies offered plenty of reasons for optimism. While none of those traits we discussed guarantee immediate production, they are the type of flashes that explain the investment Washington made in all three players. Let us know what you think about these three rookies, and the rookie class overall, in the comments below.

They will have a joint practice with the Ravens tomorrow as both team’s prepare for the preseason finale on Friday night. Head coach Dan Quinn spoke to reporters before the start of today’s practice. No players are scheduled for after practice, but reporters will talk with players on the field. Quinn talked a lot about injuries, but didn’t provide updates on several players like Odafe Oweh(calf) and Trey Amos(ankle) who have missed several weeks due to injury. Quinn said he would know more next week, which likely keeps them out of the preseason finale. Ben Sinnott suffered an oblique injury, and will also miss Friday night’s game in Baltimore. Bill Croskey-Merritt is also dealing with a lower body injury, and was doing individual drills at practice today. Quinn said they are being cautious with a lot of the team’s injuries, and most of them wouldn’t keep players out if they were preparing for a regular season game. Quinn was asked for one player that has stood out, or impress him, in training camp and the preseason, and he brought up Quan Martin. This came shortly before the team announced that veteran Will Harris was getting released. Quinn said he “felt an intensity and urgency ” from Martin this year. Quinn also talked up rookie LB Sonny Styles who has faced a lot of criticism of his performances in the the first two preseason games. Quinn said he takes command at the line of scrimmage, and he has the speed and quickness needed to excel in zone defense. title: Commanders transaction: Why Washington released veteran safety Will Harris
summary: The Commanders made several roster moves on Tuesday morning, with one bigger name lumped in with a series of lesser knowns.   Washington added an edge rusher and two safeties. They also moved an edge rusher to IR and released two safeties. This type of bottom-of-the-roster churn is common this time of year. Rarely, however, […]
full_text: The Commanders made several roster moves on Tuesday morning, with one bigger name lumped in with a series of lesser knowns. Washington added an edge rusher and two safeties. They also moved an edge rusher to IR and released two safeties. This type of bottom-of-the-roster churn is common this time of year. Rarely, however, does it include someone closer to the top of the depth chart. Will Harris was unceremoniously released on Tuesday, ending the eighth-year safety’s time in Washington. He played nine games and started them all in 2025, though a fractured fibula and a subsequent IR stint disrupted his only season with the Commanders. While more established veterans aren’t typically cut at such a random time, Harris’ release was no surprise. Mark Tyler didn’t include him in his latest 53-man roster projection, and was not alone in that analysis. Harris played a ton during the preseason when other established veterans didn’t, and not always particularly well. His game against the Lions was certainly a strike against. I was watching All-22 and came across this. Will Harris (#3) HAS to make this tackle, no excuses. pic.twitter.com/BI5NphfSID — brandon (@JayDanielsMVP) August 23, 2026 For everyone ragging on Sonny Styles here, he gets in the right run fit to allow others to make a play which is how a cohesive defense runs – Will Harris tries to make a big play and runs himself out of position https://t.co/WltJx8Jdpg — Mitchell Tischler (@Mitch_Tischler) August 25, 2026 Those mistakes look bad, especially when compared to Quan Martin’s standout preseason performances. There’s also Jeremy Reaves, who should be more involved defensively. And Tyler Owens has showed out in multiple roles during training camp, including work in the slot and in the box. Plus, Owens and fellow safety Percy Butler bring significant value to the special teams units. The Commanders sought a clear offseason upgrade by signing Nick Cross, a safety expected to be an every-down presence in the defensive backfield. Harris really didn't have a real role here anyway with Nick Cross signing here. And prior to Cross, I think majority of the people know that they should've made a better effort to keep Jeremy Chinn here after 2024 lol. — Jamual (@LetMualTellit) August 25, 2026 Overall, the Commanders just didn’t seem to need Harris anymore. Then, maybe in a sign of ominous foreshadowing, the Commanders let receiver Stefon Diggs wear Harris’ No. 3 jersey during Saturday’s game against Detroit, and let him keep it for Monday’s practice. While duplicate jersey numbers are not uncommon, you generally don’t take a veteran’s number. I don’t see Will Harris out here … seems notable since Diggs came out in the #3 prax jersey yesterday pic.twitter.com/awmOp44B63 — Mitchell Tischler (@Mitch_Tischler) August 25, 2026 While the timing of the Harris release was a surprise, cutting him was not. The team’s mind had been made up and the move came swiftly, as it did when selecting Drew Stevens at kicker. After all, there’s no sense in giving practice reps to someone you know won’t be here. Harris also gets a few extra days to survey the scene across the NFL and possibly find a new spot before a tsunami of cuts occur on Sunday. Per Washington Post reporter Tashan Reed, the Commanders spoke to Harris’ representatives and both sides decided this was the right time for a release. The team had conversations with Harris and his representation about his diminished role, per source. Ultimately, it was mutually beneficial to make this decision now and allow him to explore other opportunities before roster cut day. https://t.co/7Dwiocn4IC — Tashan Reed (@tashanreed) August 25, 2026 Was letting Will Harris go right now a smart move by Washington? Let us know in the comments below:

full_text: The Commanders have signed outside linebacker Carlos “Boogie” Basham, a move reported before Tuesday’s training camp practice. He was one of several to workout for the Commanders on Monday. Basham was one of three players signed on Tuesday, the team announced. They also added safeties Joshuah Bledsoe and Quindell Johnson. They released safeties Will Harris ( more on that move here ) and Malik Spencer and moved OLB Drake Jackson to season-ending injured reserve. We have made the following roster moves: – Signed OLB Boogie Basham, S Joshuah Bledsoe and S Quindell Johnson – Released S Will Harris and S Malik Spencer – Placed OLB Drake Jackson on the Reserve/Injured List pic.twitter.com/iacPy1f7WO — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) August 25, 2026 Update: The Commanders also announced the release of OT Foster Sarell. We have released T Foster Sarell pic.twitter.com/EgReDjCzEO — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) August 25, 2026 Basham, the Buffalo Bills second-round pick back in 2021, also played for the New York Giants and Carolina Panthers over the past five seasons. All told, he has played in 43 games , with 61 tackles, 4.5 sacks and an interception to his credit. He also played for the D.C. Defenders last season and had 24 tackles, three sacks and two forced fumbles. The Roanoke, VA, native joins the team for the preseason’s final stretch, with the Commanders banged up at his position. Hopefully, Basham can put out some quality game tape and help Washington deal with minor injuries to Odafe Oweh and K’Lavon Chaisson. The Commanders will feature their first-team players heavily during the practice week, which ends with Wednesday’s joint practice at Baltimore and sets up Friday’s exhibition finale against the Ravens. Then then team must form its initial 53-man roster by Sunday at 6 p.m. ET.

title: Commanders News: “Sonny Styles is looking fantastic this preseason”
summary: The Daily Slop – 25 August 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. full_text: The Daily Slop – 25 August 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Cover 4 Quarters Sonny Styles is already proving the hype in Washington is real This play from Styles drew the ire of fans everywhere, who immediately clamored, “Bust!” “Played like a fiddle”, and other pejorative statements. All of this outcry proved the maxim “It’s better to stay silent and be thought a fool than to speak and remove all doubts” is as true as it was when the statement was first introduced in Proverbs 17:28. On the 50-yard Joshua Dobbs TD, just a complete defensive breakdown by the #Commanders The rookie Joshua Josephs gets faked amongst other defenders. Great play by Lions. Also, Will Harris wasn’t on the same page as well. pic.twitter.com/qtnYCWGRby — brandon (@JayDanielsMVP) August 23, 2026 As the MIKE linebacker, Styles is fitting the C-gap here as his responsibility. View Link you can see he keeps his eyes on his gap responsibility until he realizes that the defensive end (#48) has completely blown his responsibility here too. It’s a read option. The defensive end is supposed to keep his eyes on the ball. #48 simply doesn’t, and Dobbs makes him pay for the mental lapse. Ideally, #48 should “squeeze and pop”, where he shuffles down the line of scrimmage to discourage the give to the running back (squeeze) before “popping” back to the quarterback by flattening out his path to interfere with his pathing. [I]t’s not a scrape exchange because nobody is filling in for Styles’ fit on this play. If there were another safety in the box, I could theoretically buy it, provided he filled in the C-gap for Styles. This play is from a 2-high shell, so the safety is deep and isn’t in the primary run fit. For my money, this touchdown lies squarely on the defensive end and the safety. The defensive end is a fifth-round rookie, so I expect some mistakes like that. The safety #3 is 30-year-old veteran Will Harris, who…I’m going to be honest: I’m not sure what he’s doing. [Styles] doesn’t give any ground to the tight end and is in prime position in his gap to take on the rusher. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Bullock’s Film Room (subscription) Commanders give glimpse of Daronte Jones’ defensive scheme vs Lions [ From BiB : The excerpt below describes the defensive play you can see in the tweet from Bullock at the bottom ] [I]t’s important to remember that in preseason, nobody wants to show anything resembling their actual schemes. However, I felt that we got a little more of a hint as to what the schemes might look like in the regular season, especially on defense. It happened early on too. On just the second snap of the game, we got a glimpse of what might be to come from Daronte Jones and his defense this year. Normally when a cornerback blitzes, you see multiple other defenders on the line of scrimmage bail out to make up the numbers in coverage, but not here. The Commanders rush their entire front five, including the three interior defensive lineman and the two edge rushers at outside linebacker. With Robertson joining them, that gives Washington six defenders blitzing, leaving just five in coverage. Having five defenders in coverage is rare, but what’s even more unique is that they don’t play man coverage behind the six-man blitz. Most offenses will associate a blitz with man coverage, because zone coverages typically rely on multiple extra defenders to cover every area on the field effectively. But the Commanders still play what appears to be zone coverage here. The safeties rotate post-snap, with Jeremy Reaves working to a deep outside third, replacing Robertson’s role in coverage. Nick Cross rotates to the deep middle of the field to play the middle third. Cornerback Mike Sainristil on the other side of the field acts like he’s playing man coverage but is actually responsible for the deep third on his side of the field. Having three deep zone defenders isn’t unusual, but typically you have four underneath defenders as part of a Cover-3 zone, or at least three underneath defenders as part of a fire zone blitz scheme. But here, Washington has just two underneath defenders in linebackers Sonny Styles and Frankie Luvu. This is a tough blitz on them because they have a huge amount of ground to try and cover underneath. But the Commanders will argue that the pressure is actually the coverage. By sending six rushers, the offense has to keep at least one eligible receiver in to protect, or they’ll be overrun. You can see on this play that both tight ends stay in to chip while the running back is slow to release as he checks protection inside. With three eligible receivers helping in protection before releasing underneath, that leaves just two receivers running routes down the field. That buys time for those six rushers to try and get to the quarterback. Rookie outside linebacker Joshua Josephs does a great job darting inside the left tackle and creating immediate pressure, which actually forced a holding call from the left tackle to prevent the sack. The quarterback feels that pressure and has to try and scramble away from it, but he has no idea Robertson is there. He runs to his left and hits a brick wall as Robertson is there to make the sack and knock the ball out. From there, it’s a fight of effort and desire to see who can jump on the ball and recover the fumble. Josephs shows great effort as he’s the one that sticks with it and fights hardest to win the ball, recovering it in the end zone for a touchdown. That was just a glimpse of what Daronte Jones has in mind for this defense. Remember, nobody wants to show anything significant at this point in the year, especially the Commanders with two new coordinators that have an advantage of opponents not knowing what schemes they’re about to face. So for Jones to show this blitz tells you it’s a very vanilla blitz for them. While the Commanders were looking to stay vanilla as possible, I felt like we got to see a small glimpse of what defensive coordinator Daronte Jones has planned for Washington's defense this year. I broke it down: https://t.co/aJbDglmEyN pic.twitter.com/hmdkGgxUew — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) August 24, 2026 Last Man Standig Dan Quinn didn’t like the ‘disarray’ in preseason Game 2. Now the Commanders get back to work Jacory Croskey-Merritt was not formally declared out of the preseason game because of injury, but he seemed to pull up at the end of a catch-and-run in Thursday’s open practice. The groin injury isn’t considered significant, I’m told, but “Bill” is the latest player the Commanders aren’t rushing back into action after an injury. Quinn said Croskey-Merritt joins a “number of guys that we hope to get into practices next week,” following a Saturday evaluation. Croskey-Merritt, Rachaad White (hamstring) and Jeremy McNichols (quad), Washington’s top three experienced backs, are all working through some form of injury. White went through individual drills Monday after sitting out practices last week. That leaves two rookies, sixth-round pick Kaytron Allen and UDFA Robert Henry Jr., along with recent signee Craig Reynolds, as the known available options against Baltimore. For more from Ben Standig, click here Sports Illustrated 3 Things We Learned From Commanders’ Added Day 15 Training Camp Practice 3. Injuries Are Still Reshaping Position Battles More than anything, Washington is still evaluating several positions while key players remain unavailable or limited. Center is the perfect example and a glaring weakness now as well . Quinn said Nick Allegretti is still not ready , while Matt Gulbin will move back exclusively to center this week after getting some work at guard. Hearing Quinn say Washington still has work to do moving forward feels like someone telling me…

title: How Jesse Minter has motivated Lamar Jackson, Ravens to 'Be The Best'
summary: Competitive drive. Player connection. Cool demeanor. All these are why the Ravens believe the 43-year-old can elevate Baltimore to a championship level.
full_text:
AT THE END of one of the Baltimore Ravens ' offseason workouts, first-year coach Jesse Minter rolled out two 16-pound medicine balls onto the practice field to get his point across.

 In an impromptu battle between the offense and defense, rookie guard Olaivavega Ioane used all his strength to throw the medicine ball farther than outside linebacker Zion Young . All of the defensive players were forced to do pushups. The offensive players' celebration was capped by rookie wide receiver Ja'Kobi Lane doing a cartwheel into a backflip.

 Throughout spring practices and training camp, the 43-year-old Minter has sprung on his players what he calls "At our best, when our best is needed" periods. The contests, which are kept secret until announced to the players at the end of practice, have included a relay featuring rookies carrying weights in both hands, a competition of one-handed catches and a race in which players push blocking sleds.

 "You never know what play is going to be the biggest play of the game," Minter told his players. "Every situation, you've got to be ready. When your number is called, you step up and make the play."

 Minter's mantra -- "Be The Best" -- is displayed in massive silver lettering next to the doors that lead to the Ravens' practice field. It's a variation of a saying by basketball coaching legend John Wooden, and it has become the foundation for this new era in Baltimore.

 Minter was hired to replace John Harbaugh, who was fired after 18 seasons, because the Ravens have struggled over the past decade to be their best when their best was needed. In eight seasons with quarterback Lamar Jackson , Baltimore dominated in the regular season but repeatedly underachieved in the playoffs because of critical mistakes and turnovers. 

 

 The Ravens believe Minter can elevate Baltimore to a championship level because of his competitive drive, his ability to connect with players and his cool demeanor.

 Unlike Harbaugh's intense, alpha-type leadership, Minter's coaching style has been described by Ravens players as calm and collected. His father, Rick, and his best friend, Ravens safeties coach P.J. Volker, can't remember a time when Minter has lost his temper.

 Throughout the spring workouts and training camp, no one has heard Minter raise his voice to the players. When Minter is unhappy with how practice is going, he huddles up the team so everyone can hear his message. Minter believes NFL teams win when there is a partnership between players and coaches.

 "He's very [focused on] connecting the team right now," wide receiver Rashod Bateman said. "I think that's something that we needed."

 One of Minter's biggest changes was how Baltimore conducted training camp. Instead of sticking with Harbaugh's scorching afternoon practices, Minter moved the start of practices to the morning to avoid the heat and players wearing down.

 Minter has also regularly cut practices short, something that rarely occurred under Harbaugh. During a practice in the middle of training camp, Minter ended practice 30 minutes early because the team had reached its goal of 100 snaps that day. This is a major shift in philosophy from Harbaugh, who wanted his players to take pride in being one of the NFL's hardest-working teams and would run as many reps as possible during the allotted practice time.

 The Ravens' players say the positive vibes stem from Minter's encouraging words. When there is a mistake, he is known to put his arm around the player to address the correction and then urge him to move on to the next snap. In discussing the changes under Minter, some in the organization have noticed less anxiety around the team.

 "It's kind of a pressure cooker that we live in on a daily basis, and he tries to take a lot of that out of it by maximizing our opportunities when we're out there -- understanding that we have to work hard, but at the same time, he takes care of us and puts us in positions to be successful and does not put everything on our plate every single day," Ravens safety Kyle Hamilton said. "It's little things each time, and I can see us slowly crescendoing throughout the season."

 

 THOSE CLOSE TO  Minter believe others mistake his mild-mannered temperament for not being competitive. Their suggestion: Ask Minter about the toughest moment of his football career.

 As the defensive coordinator for Georgia State in 2014, he watched his defense allow 69 points to rival Georgia Southern. Georgia State gave up 613 rushing yards and 10 rushing touchdowns in a game that still bothers Minter.

 "I've always felt like you can come up with answers and solutions," Minter said. "And it was just what we were trying to get accomplished wasn't translating to the players. And that was a major 'Come to Jesus' moment, I would say."

 

 Volker, who has known Minter since they were college teammates at Mount St. Joseph University, knew Minter couldn't wait for another shot at Georgia Southern.

 "We went into the lab in the offseason," Volker said. "And I'll never forget, he circled the date on the calendar. It was Dec. 5, and we were going to have the guys ready to play. And we were."

 Minter spent that offseason devising a defense that would shut down Georgia Southern's triple-option offense. He also recruited players to fit that scheme.

 That next season, Minter enjoyed one of his most satisfying wins as Georgia State defeated Georgia Southern, 34-7. Minter's defense held Georgia Southern to a season-low 203 yards of total offense. Georgia Southern coach Willie Fritz acknowledged after the game he was "outcoached."

 "That's a day I'll never forget," Minter said.

 

 IN WHAT WOULD later become a full-circle moment, Minter's first NFL coaching job came compliments of Harbaugh.

 In 2017, the Ravens had an opening for a defensive assistant. Rick Minter, Jesse's father, called Harbaugh, who had been Rick's special teams coordinator at the University of Cincinnati 20 years earlier.

 Rick Minter told Harbaugh: "He's smart, he's good looking. He can communicate. He sees the big picture."

 

 As Rick Minter put it, "I sold him on him being like John."

 But Jesse Minter quickly stood out to players by how much he listened. He often sat next to safety Eric Weddle in meetings and picked his brain about schematics and other ideas.

 "Early on, you knew he was a bright coach," Weddle said. "He thought outside the box. I just drew a great appreciation of him, his personality, his demeanor."

 In 2018, Minter was part of the staff, which included defensive coordinator Wink Martindale and linebackers coach Mike Macdonald, to overhaul Baltimore's scheme. It was during this time that Minter gives Martindale credit for valuing his input and empowering him to build more confidence in himself.

 "I just think he was very thorough and thinking things through strategically as well as breaking down opponents," Martindale said.

 Eight years later, after being defensive coordinator at Michigan and with the Los Angeles Chargers , Minter is back with the Ravens as the fourth head coach in their history. He takes over in Baltimore just months after Macdonald became the first defensive playcalling head coach to win a Super Bowl .

 Weddle believes Minter and Macdonald are "cut from the same cloth."

 "They're just very, very similar in a lot of ways," Weddle said. "And I expect to have the same impact in Baltimore as Mike has had in Seattle."

 

 IN MINTER'S INITIAL videoconference interview for the Ravens' head coaching job, he laid out his vision for the team's franchise QB to team officials.

 "Creating a partnership with Lamar as myself as a head coach is the very first priority," Minter told them. "Creating an environment where he feels like the system is helping him become the best player he can be. That he's learning a system of offense and not a collaboration of plays."

 Minter will be judged on whether he can help Jackson, one of the top players in the NFL, advance…

title: Predicting NFL teams most likely to improve in 2026 season
summary: Can the Giants and Jets improve on their awful 2025 records? Will the Chiefs, Lions and Ravens all make it back to the playoffs?
full_text:
Even by NFL standards, 2025 was a topsy-turvy season. Seven teams saw their records improve or decline by at least six wins, the most in any campaign since 2008. And though that's a little more feasible in a 17-game season than it was in the 16-game era, the 10-game improvement by the Patriots, who improved from 4-13 to 14-3, was the largest by any team since 1999, when the Colts pulled that off in Peyton Manning's second season.

 Teams hoping to emulate the Patriots might find a difficult path forward. The Pats made a major coaching upgrade by hiring Mike Vrabel, who had been one of the league's best coaches during his time with the Titans before losing a power struggle in Nashville. New England relied as heavily on free agency as any team in recent memory, with 13 of its 25 most-used players on offense and defense acquired as free agents over the previous two offseasons. And the Patriots notably had what was one of the easiest schedules in league history, facing just two teams that posted a winning record all season.

 The Patriots' path toward the Super Bowl was off my radar, and they weren't included in my annual look at teams most likely to improve at this time last year . The other six teams to jump by at least six wins, though, are all featured in one of the two columns you'll see this week. Today, we start on the rosy side and focus on the teams that are most likely to improve in 2026. And on Tuesday, we'll talk about the ones that are most likely to decline.

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 Last year's column featured the Raiders, who declined by a game, and the Giants, who improved by one win. The other three teams were much bigger successes. The Bears rode the Ben Johnson effect and a flood of takeaways on defense to an 11-6 mark after going from 5-11 in 2024. The 49ers jumped from 6-11 to 12-5. And the Jaguars made the biggest leap, going from 4-13 to 13-4 in Liam Coen's first season at the helm. All three teams made the playoffs after finishing well below .500 the previous season.

 Since 2017, this annual column has gone 35-8 (.813) in picking teams to improve on the previous season's record. The average team has gotten 3½ games better after adjusting for the 17-game schedule. And if we include our picks for teams that will decline, the back-to-back columns are a combined 69-17 (.802) in accuracy, while going 50-36 (.581) against the preseason over-under totals preserved on Pro-Football-Reference.com.

 So, recent history suggests four of the five teams listed in this year's column should get better. There's a fun mix of teams that just took a step back in 2025 and long-frustrating organizations that might exceed expectations in 2026. Let's start with the headliners from last year's decline column  who might be the most obvious pick of the bunch ...

 Note: Schedule strength is via ESPN's Football Power Index (FPI) . 

 

 
 See more: 
 Five teams set to decline 

 
 
 Jump to: 
 BAL | DET | KC | NYG | NYJ 

 
 

 

 Kansas City Chiefs 
 Record in 2025: 6-11 (1-9 in games decided by seven or fewer points) 
 Point differential in 2025: plus-34 
 Projected strength of schedule:  14th easiest

 You could have suspected things would start here. Twelve months ago, the Chiefs were coming off a 15-2 regular season and led my column on teams most likely to decline in 2025. Andy Reid's squad had gone 10-0 in games decided by seven points or fewer in 2024, an NFL record. And though anyone who has read this column annually is already familiar with the idea that teams struggle to win a significant proportion of their close games year after year, I wouldn't have blamed anyone who believed the Chiefs were an outlier.

 The 10-0 mark took Patrick Mahomes  to 43-17 in one-score contests. We've seen other generational quarterbacks -- with Tom Brady as a notable example -- win more of their one-score games than you might expect. It would have been foolish to count on the Chiefs to win every one of their one-score games again, but expecting Mahomes and the Chiefs to fall to even .500 in close games also seemed to be a bad bet.

 

 Then, the Chiefs started their 2025 season with a six-point loss to the Chargers . Kansas City lost by three to the Eagles in Week 2. The Jags ' late charge led to a Chiefs loss in Week 5. They were winning big, but when things were close, a team that had always found a way to win the close ones in 2024 found ways to lose them in 2025. The Chiefs went from 10-0 to 1-9 in one-score games between 2024 and 2025, including a 1-7 record with Mahomes under center before the star quarterback tore his left ACL .

 As you probably guessed, the 18-game swing between 2024 and 2025 is the biggest of one-score victories in league history. The previous record was 13 games by the 2022-23 Vikings, who fell from 9-0 to 4-8 in one-score games. Minnesota then followed with an 8-1 mark in 2024 before regressing to the mean and landing at 4-3 in 2025.

 The Vikings were cycling through quarterbacks for most of that time, though, and the Chiefs had Mahomes for most of last season. Most of the stars who helped the Chiefs to three consecutive Super Bowl appearances were back in 2025, too. And though the Chiefs were down to third-stringers at QB and left tackle by the end of the season, they were about average in terms of season-long health on offense and even had the league's healthiest defense, per the FTN Football Almanac 's adjusted games lost metric.

 Did the Chiefs just play significantly worse? By advanced metrics, the answer to that question is ... not really. The 2024 Chiefs finished the regular season eighth in DVOA, pointing to a good team that had remarkable luck in one-score games. And though the 2025 Chiefs understandably faded after Mahomes gave way to  Gardner Minshew II  and Chris Oladokun at quarterback, they ranked eighth in DVOA through the game against the Chargers in Week 15, when Mahomes suffered his ACL injury.

 The 2024 Chiefs outscored their opponents by 59 points, or roughly 3.5 points per game. And if we don't include the post-Mahomes games, the 2025 Chiefs outscored their opponents by 60 points, which is just under 4.3 points per game. Point differential suggests those teams should roughly expect to get about the same number of wins over a full season with an average amount of luck and timing.

 To put that into context over 17 games, let's look at teams that outscored their opponents by a margin between three and five points per game in a season. Since 1990, 117 teams have fit into that window. The best record produced by any of those teams is 15-2, which matches the Chiefs' 2024 record. The Chiefs were 6-8 with Mahomes in the lineup, and that would have been a .428 winning percentage over a full season. That would be the worst winning percentage produced by any of those three-to-five-point-differential teams over a full campaign. In other words, the 2024 Chiefs got the best recorded results out of being a pretty good team since 1990, and the 2025 Chiefs -- even with Mahomes -- were getting the worst results of any team at that level in recent history before his injury.

 Even if the Chiefs produce average results with that sort of point differential in 2026, they should be back in the postseason. Are there reasons to be concerned that they won't match up to that underlying level of play? Maybe. To start, Mahomes is returning from the torn ACL. Though the soon-to-be 31-year-old quarterback is still in contention to start the season on the active roster, it's difficult to imagine that he won't feel some sort of disruption or struggle coming back from his first significant injury as a pro. At the very least, Mahomes' legendary ability to scramble and extend plays might be limited early in 2026.

 

 The defense has also lost key players in the secondary, with Trent McDuffie dealt to the Rams, Jaylen Watson joining the Rams in free agency and starting safety Bryan Cook inking a deal with the Bengals. The…
